### THE DECRETALL EPISTLES.

These Epistles decretall which passe under the names, Clement, Evarist, Telesphorus, Higinus, Anicetus, Soter, Calixtus, Urban, Pontian, Anterus, Fabian, &c. and Sylvester, are all forged: and that for sixe reasons.[801] First, all these epistles had one and the same author, for they are all written in the same style and forme of writing; and the same phrases are often repeated in divers epistles. Now it is a thing impossible, for so many Bishops to speake all just after one forme, though they should labour to imitate one another. 2. Many things of these Epistles are written so farre from the true phrase of the Latine, that they are mecrely barbarous: as this: Episcopi sunt obedendi, diligendi, & summopere venerandi, & non detrahendi vel lacerandi: and this, Patres omnes sunt venerandi, non respuendi, aut infidiandi, &c. 3. These epistles in their quotations of holy Scripture doe follow Hieromes translation, which none of the Popes that these decrees are fathered upon, ever sawe: for it was not then extant. 4. There is not one epistle almost of them all, but containeth some things expresly against the credit of all Historicall truth, for they speake of the Primacy and rule of the Church of Rome, ordination of Bishops, and of their immunities, of the accusation & degradation of priests, and of appealing to the sea of Rome, whereas in the three first ages, because of the multitude of persecutions, little respect (as Sylvius saith) was had unto the Church of Rome. 5. So saith Cusanus in his booke de concordia Catholica lib.3 cap 2. and Bellarmine de Pontifice, lib.2. c.14. confesseth, that some errors have crept into these Epistles, and that hee dares not affirme them to be infallibly theirs, whose name they beare: & Isidore in his preface before the Councils, doth not mention them all; Eusebius speaks only of the epistles of Clement & Victor, which yet are not now extant. Damasus writing of his predecessors, never saith word of these epistles. No more doth Hieron.

Besides, the decretall epistles of the Popes (extant in the tomes of the Councils) from Sylvester unto Gregory the first, & so forward, are all either counterfeit, or justly suspected.

This is plainly shewed by the grosse absurditie of their stile, in the most of them, by their unapt alledging the Scriptures, & their desire of rule over the Catholike Church. For at this they doe ayme, namely, to erect and protect the supremacy of the Church of Rome. Chiefly these following.

1 Marke his Epistle unto the Bishops of Egypt. He saith that the Romane Church did never erre, nor ever hereafter shall erre. But that opinion of the immobilitie of the Romane faith, was not admitted into the world unullin these latter times. Catherinus in Gal. 2.

2 Julius his first Epistle unto the Bishops of the East for Athanasius. This disagreeth quite from the true copie which is in Socrates l.2.c.15. and in Sozomen. l.3.c.8. His second also is foolish and frivolous.

3 Liberius his answer to Athanasius, and his Epistle unto all Bishops.

4 Felix his Epistles to the Synod of Alexandria.

5 Stevens unto Damasus, and another of Damasus unto Steven Bishop of Africa, wherein there are these words of new Latine Charitative, compassibiliter, ordinabiliter, prafixi fratres, innotuisse, for indicasse. Such like is that of his. [ad Episcopos Numidiae] and another [ad Episcopos Illyricos.]

6 Syricius his first Epistle unto Himerius Bishop of Tarracon. The barbarousnesse of the style maketh it suspected, as in these words. In ergastulis autem suis tales personas retrudendas, ut tantum facimus continua lamentatione deflentes purificato to poenitudinis igne possint decoquere. Besides, he imperiously commandeth the Bishop of Tarracon to publish his decrees to be observed of all the Bishops: But the Church of Rome as then had no such jurisdiction.

Of no greater value is his Epistle to the Millaners; nor the 3. and 4. to the B. of Africa,

7 Two Epistles of Anastasius. The date, and the Consuls hereto subscribed, disagree from all true histories. In the first you shall finde these words. Quasi ad caput charitative mittere non dubitetis. And hee commandeth with Apostolike authority, standum esse ad adlectionem Evangelij.

8 The Epistles under Innocentius the first his name, are justly called in question, because there are in them many traditions, which unto the Divines of those times were altogether unknowne. And besides there are whole Paragraphes put into them which are extant as well in the latter Popes writings, as in the former. The third Epistle to Exuperius, maketh mention of five bookes of Salomon: the 22. speaketh of the Bishops Miter, which the Church then knew not. And the Epistle unto the Council of Carthage is very foolish and idle.

The Epistles also of Innocentius which are the 91. and the 93. among the Epistles of S. Augustine, are counterfeit. Erasmus.[802]

9 Sixtus the third his Epistle unto the Easterne Bishops, hath these words: Valentinianus Augustus nostra authoritate Synodum congregari jussit. Most foolishly! Valentinian could call a Council by his owne authority, and needed no Popes assistance, the Epistle therefore is forged. In his third Epistle, de [ilegible] doctoribus &c., these words, [Semper tamen Purgatorij locum excipio, in quo animae hominum corporibus soluta ad tempus purgantur] are thrust in by some other, for they have no coherence at all, either with the precedent, or consequent clause: for Sixtus saith, there is but two places, Heaven and Hell, and that out of the kingdome of God there is no salvation.

10 Hilarius his Epistles.

11 Anastasius his Epistle unto Anastasius the Emperour, hee warneth him to obey the Apostolike admonition, viz. the Popes decrees; whereas the Popes of those dayes obeyed the Emperours decrees, [ilegible].

12 Pope John the first his 2. Epistle is opposite unto the history of that time.

13 Felix the IV. his Epistles, the second whereof beginneth thus. Quoniam importabilibus verbis garrulasti.

14 Boniface the 2. his Epistle, and the interpretation of Carthage thereunto annexed doth [ilegible] mention made of the Prince Iustinian, whereas Boniface, Bishop of Rome, [ilegible] [ilegible] [ilegible] the Church [ilegible] [ilegible] house [ilegible].

15. Pius his first Epistle is very trifling, [ilegible] [ilegible] that Churches may be rectified, and consecrated with the Masse onely, without any sprinkling of holy water. His third is so confusedly placed together, that it is impossible to make true sense of it.

16 Iulius the third his Epistle.

17. Benedict the first his Epistles: Part of it is a fragment of Alexander the first, his first epistle decretall: the other part is almost the whole fourth chapter of the first Epistle unto Timothy.

Gregory the third, his third Epistle (tom.3. Concil.) ad Episcopos Bavariae, disagreeth from the copie which is in Aventinus Annales, lib.3.

Zacharies fifth Epistle (tom.3. Concil.) contained frivolous answers to most foolish questions. One thing chiefly to be noted is, his command of the time when to eate bacon. His sixth Epistle is corrupt by some filthy interpreter. Catalogus testium.

18 Nicholas his Epistles unto the Emperour Michael. Therein hee said that godly Emperours never would command the Priests, but intreat them as Fathers. But Eusebius saith otherwise, lib.10. chapter 5. and Nicephorus, lib.7. cap.43. These say that Constantine the Emperour commanded Miltiades Bishop of Rome to judge the cause of Caecilianus Bishop of Carthage. The epistle of the Synod of Alexandria to Pope Felix is counterfeit, and full of lyes.

Hilarius his epistle (the 88. amongst Augustines) is not rightly ascribed unto Hilary of Poictou.[803] Erasmus. The epistle also unto Apra his daughter, containeth nothing worthy of Hilarius, nor the hymne unto her.

The history of Ambrose his life, attributed unto Paulinus, is a fiction.[804] Erasmus in his preface unto Ambrose his workes.

### EVODIVS.

Two bookes of the miracles of S. Stiven, extant in Augustine tenth tom. are both forged.[805] Tritemius indeed saith, that he wrote a volume of the miracles done in Africke by the reliques of Steven the Martyr, which reliques Orosius the Priest caried thither: But these bookes now extant containe no such matter, neither are they mentioned in any Author at all.

### [ilegible]

### IOHN CASSIANVS, and FAVSTVS RHEGIENSIS.

Both these authors bookes Gelasius in a Councell of 70. Bishops did condemne, And with reason.[809] For the first wrote against Prosper, & the second against Fulgentius, concerning the Predestination of the Saints, and the good of perseverance. Besides, Faustus was condemned by Petrus Diaconus, lib. de Incar. Hormisda Pope in his Epistle in 5. Tom. Biblioth. Ado in Chronicis: and Trithemius in Fausto. And therefore Driedo and Ruardus Tapper in approving Faustus his writings doe shew themselves halfe Pelagians.

### THEODORETVS.

His 12. bookes, De curatione Graecarum affectionum, are suspected,[810] because Nicephorus in his catalogue of Theodorets labours nevertheless mentioneth them. And these bookes make for the Invocation of Saints, which Theodoret upon the second of the Colossians, doth condemne:

His Epistles also unto Leo and Renatus are doubtfull.

His booke De Sanctis hath some things inserted by others.

### LEO.

These workes of his beare a counterfeit name.[811]

A Sermon upon All-Saints day, either wholly forged, or at least in the title. For this Feast had his originall from Boniface the 4. about the yeare of our Lord 610. long after Leo. Petrus de Natalibus, lib.10. cap.1.

His 5. Sermon of Lent, is Augustines 63. De Tempore, and his eight Sermon is Augustines 33. de Tempore.

Some of his Epistles, as the 84. and the 92. are no where extant, but in Gratian, who (like a notorious falsifier) thrust many workes upon the Fathers which they never were authors of. And it is a strange thing that Leo should offer to send his imperious Edicts through Europe, Asia, and Affricke, when as hee was constrained of necessity to make a supplication unto the Emperour for the calling a Councill within Italy. And hereby it is plaine, that his 84. and 46. Epistles are either counterfeit or at least corrupted: because hee arrogateth the fulnesse of power in soveraigne and far distant regions, and enjoyneth Anatolius Bishop of Constantinople to execute his commission in the beginning of the 46. Epistle. But the Fathers of the first generall Councill, expounding and confirming that which formerly had beene defined in the first Councill of Constantinople, and in the Councill of Chalcedon, say thus in the 36. chapter: Renewing the Decrees of the 150. Fathers that met in this royall citie of Constantinople, & of the 630. Bishops which assembled at Chalcedon, will likewise determine, that the Sea of Constantinople hath equall priviledges and honour with the Sea of Rome, and in all Ecclesiasticall matters be advanced, and great honour and reverence as it, being next unto it.

The Epistles of Iohn Pope, and Iustinian, extant in the Code, lib.1. tit.4. de Summa Trinitate, are of doubtfull credit.[812] For first, Iustinian saith there, that hee hath laboured, that all the Priests of the Easterne jurisdiction should bee obedient unto the Church of Rome. But all histories say, that this was Phocas his deed. Ado Viennensis, chronicall anno 604. Tom. Carnotensis, in Christi Platina in Bonifacio tertio. It is also ascribed unto Michael Psellus Theologus. Besides, in this Epistle the Pope is called the head of all Churches. But the contrarie is to bee seene in Gregory the fourth his Registrum, epist. 31. 34. 36. 38. Thirdly, this Epistle and the other of Iohn, are not extant in the old Manuscripts: witnesse Alcuin, Pavery, lib.5. cap.23.

Articus his Epistle in the end of the Councill of Chalcedon is a counterfeit. Looke Iunius his Animadversions in Bellarmine de Pontif. Rom. lib.1. cap.14. & lib.2. cap.23.

The Epistle of the said Councill unto Leo is such another. Newly found (as is pretended) in the Library of the Friars preachers at Coleine.

__________
[811] Ann. 450.
[812] Ann. 450.

### GELASIVS.

The booke of the two Natures, Bellarmine denieth to be written by Gelasius the Pope, De Pontif. lib.4. cap.10.[813] And Melchior Canus loc. comm. lib.6. cap.8, yet they hold it the worke either of Gennadius, or Gelasius Bishop of Caesarea.

__________
[813] Ann. 456.

### VIGILIVS.

His epistle unto Theodosius, Anthemius, Severus, Eutychian hereticks, wherein hee professeth himselfe to be of their opinion, is censured to be a counterfeit, by Baronius, tom.7. upon the yeare 538. and after a sort by Bellarmine de Pontifice lib.4. cap.10. But the epistle is described by Liberatus, and is extant in the 22. chapter of his Breviarie, and is also in the Chronicle of Victor. The same doth testifie that it was written after Vigilius his ordination, and therefore Bellarmine erreth in holding the contrarie.

### ANDREAS CRETENSIS.

His Encomium de dormitione Sanctae deiparae, cap.6.[814] maketh mention of the feast of the Assumption of Marie, which was not instituted untill the yeare of our Lord 595. many yeares after this authors death: therefore these orations seeme forged.

### THE COVNCILL OF AGATHA

### EVSEBIVS EMISSENVS.

The Homilies under this name were not written by Eusebius of Emesa in Greece, but by a certaine frenchman, as appeareth in the homily unto Blandina. Fulke. Bellarmine confesseth this also, De extrema unctione lib.1. chap.5. Looke also in the same Bellarmine de sacram. Eucharist. lib.2. cap.29.

The sermon of the feast of the Nativity, beginning Nativitas Domini,[816] extant amongst Fulgentius his workes, is ascribed unto Augustine, and is his 15. sermon de Tempore. And in some Manuscripts it is fathered upon Severianus.

The booke of his Dialogues is doubted of:[817] it is stuffed full of Italian wonders, and is not consonant unto the rest of Gregories writings, neither in matter nor forme. Chemnitius.

### THE 6. SYNOD.

The canons of this Council in Trullo are condemned by the Papists as forged, but in the second Nicene Council they are commanded to be observed, and are by Gratian himselfe approved, dist. 16. capite. Sextus Master Beza citeth an old glosse of Balsamon, taken out of a very old Manuscript. The words in English are these. And this is also a generall Councill: For although the Bishops of the West, namely, the Latines and Italians (to whom this Councill in some canons gives a sore blow) doe urge it very earnestly, that it is no universall Councill, nor that the Popes Delegate was there present: because that there is another 6. Councill held under Constantine surnamed long bearded, (as it is reported) and that this was held long after by the command of Iustinian Rhinotmetus. But I, not induring this, and looking nearer into the coherence of this matter, and into the canons orderly following, written in these words: The holy and generall Councill defineth thus and that: letting passe the moderne canons, which are neither subscribed by the Kings, nor the Fathers, that held the Councill: taking under examination the most ancient copies of these Canons. I found amongst the names subscribed unto this Councill in Trullo, that there were present in that Councill, both the Popes Deputies, one, Basilius, Primate of Cortina in Crete, and another who was Bishop of Ravenna, and not onely them, but also other of the Popes Legates being Bishops of Thessalonica, Sardinia, Heraclea in Thrace, and Corinth. Thus much Balsamon. And Bartholomew Carranza writeth thus. In the volume of the Councills printed at Coleine, there are nine Canons ascribed unto the sixt Synod, whereas we know that the 6. Synod which was called under Constantine, set forth no Canons; but afterward under Iustinian, there were 227. Fathers gathered together in the Emperours Pallace at Constantinople, and they set forth the 102. following Canons. This is affirmed by the Fathers of the 7. Councill held at Nicea under Constantine the sonne of Leo, and Irene his mother in 5. Act. of the said Councill, and more at large in the 6. Act. tom. 1. In both places citing the 82. of these Canons. Besides Nicholas the 1. maketh mention of these canons, in his Epistle unto Michael the Emperour, as also Anastasius Abbat, and librarie keeper unto the sea Apostolike, in the preface of the 8. Synod, saying: Seeing that the 6. Councill set forth no rule at all, but onely the Creede, it is certaine that the Canons by him alledged, were set forth privately and by themselves long after the 6. Councill. Moreover, the Fathers of both Empires called together at the Councill of [ilegible], these 102 Canons in the 5. Session. Gratian also in the decree citeth some of these Canons, and [ilegible] them unto that 6. Councill. Thus much Gratian, Dist. 6. cap. Sextus. Adrian the 1. Pope saith: I receive the 6. holy councill with all the Canons. And the same Adrian in his Epistle unto Tarasius hath these words: In the Divine and fully published Canons of the 6. Councill, &c. Surius granteth that the 9. Canons are fathered upon the 6. Councill, [ilegible] counterfeit.

### THE 2. COVNCILL OF NICE

This Councill, being wholly for Image worship,[820] [ilegible] impious and idolatrous, and [ilegible] rejected by the Bishops of the West, as witnesseth Aventine in his Annals, l.4. ### CAROLVS MAGNVS.

There is a booke of his against the Councill of Nice, which the Papists doe say is forged, but without any ground at all. For Hincmar Archbishop of Rhemes in his booke against Hincmar Bishop of Landuna maketh mention of this booke, and saith hee read it when hee was a boy in the Emperours Palace, and cited almost word by word the 28. chapter lib.4. Besides Augustine Steuchus, keeper of the Laterane library at Rome, doth testifie in publike writing, that the copie of this book is there extant written in old Lombard letters. Thus much out of the most learned Hospinian.

### LVDOVICVS PIVS.

Charlemaines sonne.[821] His donation, wherein he gives Rome, and the Popes election unto the Pope and Citizens of Rome, dist.63. cap. Ego Ludovicus, &c. is a meere forgery. For Paschalis being forced by the people to take the Popedome upon him without the Emperours authority, cleareth himselfe by his legate unto the Emperour Ludovicus Pius, and layeth all the fault upon the Clergie and people. Th'Emperour was herewith satisfied, but he sent a sharpe and severe command unto the people to beware ever after to offer like injury unto the Imperiall majesty. Sabellicus Ennead 8. lib.9. Platina in Paschalis his life. Molinaeus the Civilian thinkes that some librarist of the Popes tooke paines to force this Donation, and therefore that just suspition may disanull the credit thereof.

Besides, the Canon Dist.63. cap. Ego Ludovicus, is contrary to the Canon Dist.63. cap. Cum Hadrianus. For if Lodwick the first, have given away his freedome of the Popes election, why should Lodwick the 2. his nephew think himselfe any way wronged therein?

__________
[821] Ann. 810.

### Othe the Emperours oath.

In the decree, distinction 63. chap. ubi domino, there is an oath set downe taken by this Emperours legates in his name, unto Iohn then Pope. Now all this is as true as that the sea burneth. For Otho, comming unto Rome, as the Soveraigne Lord and commander of the Pope, deposed Iohn from that dignitie for his villanies, all the whole city, clergy and laitie approving and applauding his justice in this doing. Witnesse, Liutprandus, & Paulus Diaconus, hist.lib.6. as also Theod. à Niem.

### ANASTASIVS.

There is a booke of the lives of the Popes under this mans name,[822] wherein are divers errors set down, not justifiable by any ancient or grave authours testimony in the world: many Chronicle slippes, some contrarieties, and some impossibilities. Baronius thinkes it done by divers, at least by two severall authors: It is in some places altogether depraved by the forged additions and detractions of others, by reason of the extreme ignorance of former ages. The first part is fathered upon Damasus by Platina, Trithemius, & Onuphrius: It swarmeth with absurd barbarismes and solaecismes. Thus much Albinus.

### JEFFREY ARTHVR of Monmouth.

His foure bookes of the Brittish affaires, are thus censured by William of Newbery: There is (said hee) a certaine writer of late come forth, telling many ridiculous tales of the Brittaines, extolling them (with impudent fooleric) farre above the Macedons and Romanes: hee is called Jeffery, surnamed Arthur, because the olde Brittish tales of Arthur are by him augmented, and with a little rhetoricall paint, published as histories of authenticall credit. Nay besides and about this, hath published for most impeachable and impregnable verities and prophecies, containing most deceitfull divinations of one Merlin, to which he hath also added much of his owne fancings, and his translation of them into Latine. Againe, how egregiously impudent is he in farcing in fictions into his booke which he calleth the Brittish history, no man that readeth it, (unlesse wholly ignorant of antiquity) can but see. For he that knoweth not the halfe of things, quickly giveth way to the current of illuding fables, and fabulous illusions. I omit to recapitulate his fictions of the Brittaines gests before Cesars conquest: streames flowing either from his owne invention, or els derived by him (as through aleaden conduits) from other braines into his booke, as immoveable verities. Thus much Newbery, somewhat sharpely, considering his own workes are subject to the same venture that so roughly thundereth upon Arthur, for he himself oftentimes leaves the true tract of histories, to search in trifling fables into the body of his history of the affaires of England.

### NICEPHORVS CALLISTVS.

An author fraught with fables, &c.[829] telleth a tale of Christs image sent of him unto Abagarus: But Eusebius found no such thing in the treasuries of Edessa: libro primo hist. in fine.

All ancient authors, uncited of some succeeding writer, and unauthorized by some good author, are either really forged, or by the Church unallowed: and therefore of more doubtfull credit: and such is Ludgarus of S. Suiberts miracles, &c.

Also all bookes 1. that have their originall from some Romish librarist. 2. that are extant onely in the Vatica or Lateran library. 3. or onely in the Monkes cloysters, all such wee justly suspect.

What soever any olde writer hath unfitly set downe, concerning any matter of faith, were it written before any heresie was risen up about that matter, it is to be fitly and favourably expounded: but if it were written after any such heresie, it is flatly and fairely to be rejected.

[829] An.1300.

## III. The causes of the Corruption of the Apostolike Religion.

1 The doctrine of religion is by many, wrung, and wrested unto the opinions of the Heathen. So doth Cassander testifie in the appendix of the defence of his booke de officio pii viri. We cannot (quoth he) deny, but that the auncient Christians (with a wonderfull consent) have affirmed that of the lawes of their religion, which both the Romans, and other nations in elder times have affirmed of their lawes: viz. that they were partly written, and partly unwritten, [griego]. The Greeks themselves doe use these words: even Clem. Alexand. Basil, Epiphan & Dionysius. And the Fathers (lest the doctrine of the Church should seeme too harsh,) doe twine it towards naturall reason, and physicall arguments: and in the questions of sinne, free will, and faith, they argue more like Philosophers then divines: as for example, Athanasius in his booke against Idols, and Clement in the 2. of his Stromata.

The councels of the supererogation are nothing else, but the Philosophers [griego] or decorum. The doctrine of Purgatory came into the Church out of the Heathen writers: for the Philosophers and the Poets were the first that ever wrote of the paines of Purgatory after death: as Plato in his 10. booke, de Republica. Virgill in his 6. of Æneads, and Ovid in his Metamorphosis, l.15. The Platonists (saith Augustine de civit. Dei lib.21. cap.13.) although they will have no sinne unpunished, yet all those punishments they will have to tend unto reformation, whether they bee inflicted by law divine, or humane, in this life, or after death.

2 The rites and customes of the heathen (with some little change) have bin brought into the forme of Gods worship, and that by Christians. It was a custome with many to banquet upon Martyrs solemnities, and this was fetched from an olde ethnicke custome. August. confession. l.6. c.2. Gregory Thaumaturg changed the Gentiles solemnities into the Martyrs feasts. Gregory Nyssenus in his life, saith thus: He suffered the celebrations of the Martyrs memories, lest the unskilfull multitude should (through desire of vaine delight) persist in the adoration of their gorgeous idolatry. Theod. de Euang. verit. cognit. l.3. saith, for the Basilia Diasia, & Dionisia, that is, the feasts of Jupiter and Bacchus; the people doe now make their banquets to solemnize the memories of Peter, Paul, Thomas, Sergius, Marcellus, Leontius, Anthonine, Maurice, and other such holy Martyrs. Painting and Imagerie was an heathenish custome. Eusebius, l.7. c.17. hist. Eccles. also to burne incense, and light tapers unto the Images. Cicero. offic. lib.3. yearely vigils were used of the Gentiles before they came into the Church, as appeareth by Suetonius in Vespasians life, c.7. as also sprinkling of holy water: Juvenal, Satyr. 6. which Sex. Empiricus expresly calls a heathenish custome. l.6. c.6. Also lighting of candles by day light: Seneca. l.4. epist. 15. also shaving of crownes: Apuleius de asino aureo, l.11. The priests of Isis (quoth he) had their haire shaven, and their crownes very smooth. Rufinus hist. l.9. c.29. saith, that for Serapis his brest plate, every one painted the crosse upon the postes, entries, windowes, walls, and pillars: and that Constantine used this signe of the crosse in his ensigne, Sozomene testifieth, l.1. c.5.

3 The Church hath resumed the abolished customes and ceremonies of the Iewes; as the making of their holy vestiments according unto the Priests of Moses law, Alcuinus de offic. divin. also Amalarius de offic. Eccl. l.2. c.22. Gratian de consecr. Dist.1. saith, that the consecrations, and holy unctions are to be made and performed according unto the prescript of Moses, and the imitation of the Levites. The licence & too free libertie which the Church used in these three things, hath bene the cause of all these corrupted festers now predominant therein, and rankling the chiefe and choise parts thereof.

## The Demonstration of the Probleme, or Position.

The Demonstration of the Probleme shall bee shewed in these positions following, which I have composed of the chiefest places of divinity, which are now in controversie. And the scope of all them is this, to shew and proove, that the Religion at Rome now professed, is falsely called Catholike. And the summe of my Demonstration tends to shew, that the chiefe and proper heads thereof, either 1. were not received from the times of Christ, or his Apostles, or 2. if they were received thence, yet not as Articles of faith, but only as Opinions and probable Conjectures; or 3. that in all places the Purest Churches never held them in the same sense that the Papists held them in the Councill of Trent.

### Holy Scripture.

The auncient and Christian Church hath acknowledged the Iewes Canon of the olde Testament to bee true and perfect, excluding wholly from thence the Bookes of Tobie, Iudith, Wisedome, Ecclesiasticus, and the Maccabees.

Testimonies.

Besides these (saith Athanasius, in Synopsi,) There are other bookes of the olde Testament which are not canonicall, but onely read by the Catechumenists, as the booke of Wisedome, Ecclesiasticus, &c. Of these (saith Cyril of Hierusalem, Catech.4.) reade the 22. bookes, but meddle not with the Apocrypha, meditate diligently upon those Scriptures which the Church doth confidently reade, and use no other. The Apostles and Bishops at the first sowing of the word, who left us these bookes, were farre wiser, far holier then thou art: therefore since thou art the sonne of the Church, do not break the bounds they have set thee in: and as I said before, study the 22. bookes of the old Testament. These are they (saith Cyprian, or Ruffinus in exp. Symb. of the Iewes Canon) which the Fathers have put into the Canon, by which we must lay the foundation of our faith: yet note this, that there are other bookes also called by the Fathers, Ecclesiasticall, not Canonicall, and such is the Wisedome of Salomon, and another of Iesus Syrach, as also the bookes of Toby, Judith, & the Maccabees. In the new Testament, the booke called Pastor—, all which bookes they would have read in the Church, but not alleadged for confirming any point of faith. Epiphan. l. de pond. & mens. after he hath reckoned up the Canon, thus censureth the books of the Wisedome of Salom. and Eccles. They are fit and profitable, but not reckoned amongst those which are approoved by the Church: and therefore they were neither laid up in Arca, nor in the Arke of the Testament. The same words are in Damasc. And Nazianzene doth certainly determine of the Canon in his verses of the true books of holy Scriptures. In English, thus.

In our old Testament two and twentie bookes are set, According to the number of the Hebrew Alphabet.

Looke also in the same Nazian. his Iambicke poesie unto Seleucus, of good education. Hierome saith, in prolog. Galeato in lib. Reg. The Wisedome of Salomon, Iesus Syrach, Iudith, and Toby, are not in the Canon. And in another place, Praef. in I. Salo. As the Church readeth the bookes of Iudith, Toby, and Maccabees, and yet allowes them not for canonicall, so also we reade these two (the books of Wisedome and Syrach) for the edifying of the people, but not for confirmation of any Ecclesiasticall opinion. And in a third place, Praef. in Esdram & Nehem. ad Dominionem & Rogatianum: what books soever are not from the Hebrewes, & among the 24. old ones, are wholly to be rejected. This opinion of Hierome doth Lyra, Prolog. in Apocryph. Dionysius Carthusianus, & Hugo Cardinalis, Prol. in Iosu. follow. Let us take a testimony (saith Gregory, in Iob. l.19. c.17.) out of the Maccabees, which although they be not Canonicall, yet were set forth to edifie the Church. Toby, Judith, and the Maccabees, (saith Radulphus in Levit. l.14. c.1.) are not of any authority though they be read for the instruction of the Church. After the Authentike bookes (saith Petrus Cluniacensis, epist. 2. l.1.) there remaines other sixe to be spoken of, viz. Wisedome, Syrach, Toby, Iudith, and the two of the Maccabees, and these though they could not attaine to the credit & authoritie of the former, yet for their commodiousnes, & good worth, they have deserved admittance of the Church. Caietan in the end of Hester, saith, that seaven chapters of Hester, the books of Toby, Judith, Wisedome, Ecclesiasticus, and the Maccabees, are all Apocrypha. Charles Sigon. Com. in Sever. Sulpitium, denies the Macchabees to be canonicall, because of the dissonance of the style from the rest, and seemes to preferre the history of Iustine before it. Hierome saith, in Praefat. in Iudith: that the Nicene Councill reckoned Iudith amongst the holy Scriptures: therefore that Synod helde all the rest of the Apocrypha as unworthy of allowance in the Church; yet is not that certaine which Hierome affirmeth of this book: for his words are, we reade the councill to have reckoned it: but Athanasius, present at that Councill, utterly refuseth it. Also the Councill of Laodicea, in ca. 59. decreed, that no part of the old Testament should be read in the Church, but onely the Hebrewes canonicall Scriptures. Indeed the 3. Councill of Carthage, in the 47. Canon, numbereth all the aforenamed bookes amongst the holy Scriptures: But I say that the Catalogue of the bookes of that Councill, is either counterfeit, or justly doubted of, for 1. this Canon which is reckoned for the 47. of this Councill, is in some bookes the 24. Canon of another Councill under Boniface, as Surius will testifie. 2. In this Canon are allowed 5. bookes of Salomon: whereas there are not so many. 3. The Canons in Trullo approove both the Laodicean Councill, & this, which should not have beene done if they had determined just contraries: the one making that apocryphall, which the other makes Canonicall. I think the Councill of Carthage held all bookes Canonicall, which the ancient Fathers admitted to be read in the Church.

2. The booke of Baruch hath bin held apocryphal, both by the Fathers & Councils even to the yeere 1439. at which time the Florentine Councill canonized it: and yet did Driedo deny it to be Canonicall after this D. dogm. Eccl. lib.1. cap.4.

3. Hesters last 7. chapters. Daniels hymne of the children, the history of Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, are all rejected as counterfeits by the Fathers. Hierome praef. in Daniel. calls the history historie of Susanna, Bel, and the Dragon fables, and saith they beare not the authoritie of holy Scripture. And so he saith, Euseb. Apollinaris, and Methodius doe all judge.

The author of the booke de mirabilibus scripturae, in S. August. l.2. c.3. saith, that concerning the other denise of Lyons, and the transportation of Abacuc, in the tale of Bel & the Dragon, nothing is put in this ranke, because they are not contained in the divine Scriptures. And Sixtus Senensis, Bibliotheca lib.1. cap.8. rejecteth the 7. chapters of Hester, & the historie of Susanna, as additions.

4 The word Canonical is vsed by the Fathers in two senses, viz. absolutely, and respectively, [griego]. That which is absolutely Canonicall is the perfect rule both of faith and discipline. Respectively Canonicall is that worke, wherein are contained some sentences taken out of the writings absolutely Canonicall, and some historicall concerning the Church of God, and are therefore allowed to bee read in the Church at publike meetings. And in this sense it is opposite onely to prophane and heathenish workes. In this sense are these Apocryphall bookes called Canonicall, and divine, or, of divine authority by August. De civ. Dei lib.18. c.36. cum c.23. l.2. contra 2. Epist. Gaudentij: and Hierome, praef. in Machab. And in this sense doth the Councell of Carthage in the afore cited canon acknowledge all those for Canonicall Scriptures, which (saith it) wee haue received from the Fathers, to bee read in the Church. And indeed, when as the Fathers doe cite these Apocrypha, they doe not alleage them as properly Canonicall, but onely as historicall. Ambrose lib. de bono mortis & lib.2. in Lucam, cite h the 4 booke of Ezra, yet who is hee that holdeth this booke for Canonicall? So is the third of Ezra, and Hermes his booke called Pastor, oftentimes alleadged by the ancient writers, and yet are Apocrypha. By the Canons of the Apostles, Can.84. the 3 booke of the Maccabees is Canonicall, but not by the Councell of Trent. Bellarmine saith, that the decrees of the Popes are by Gratian called holy Scriptures, but [griego], that is, abusively, to distinguish them from prophane writings: and Canonicall to distinguish them from the Fathers holy workes, which are neither rules for our faith, nor haue power to bind vs to beleeue them. For although (quoth he) the Canons of Popes, and Councels are distinguished from & set after the holy Scriptures, yet in their kinde, they both are & may be called holy and Canonicall writings, — as Innocentius cap. Cum Martha, extra de celebr. Missarum, calleth that sentence of Augustines holy Scripture, (he injureth a martyr, that prayeth for a martyr.) And in this sense doth Damasus call the Canons of the Apostles Canonicall.

5. The auncient Fathers, and the most learned of their successors, doe hold the Hebrew and Greeke text of the holy Scriptures to be uncorrupted and pure. This not one denies. Hier. in c.6. Isa. condemneth them that say that the Hebrew bookes are corrupted. The same Father will have more credit given to the original, then to the translator. Ep. ad Lucin. de opt. gen. interp. In c.3. Mat. ep. ad August. 89. praef. in 4 Euan. Augustine also, De civ. Dei l.15. c.13. saith, That when a diversity is found in the bookes, trust that language from whence it is knowne, to haue beene first translated. So sayth Ludovicus Vives upon this place of Augustine. And Augustine himselfe in divers other places, viz. Ep. 108. Tract. 3. in Ioan. [ilegible] Christ, l.c.11. Arias Montanus saith plainly that the Iewes never corrupted the Hebrew booke which wee now haue; and if there were any change, yet was there not one word, one letter, one tittle which was not kept in the masorah called Mazzoreth, and therefore he calleth that Mazzoreth a faithfull custody.

6. The Fathers before Gregory the first, neuer vsed the vulgar translation, which is now said to be of Hieromes correction, by Damasus his command.

1, Tertullian against Marcion vsed it not.

7 Gregory often followeth that translation, even the errours of them that copied it out as Luke 15. evertit domum, for evertinbum. 34. in Evangel. Therefore the Latine translation fathered on Hierome, had not the gosting, neither was it preferred in the Romane Church before other, till about the time of Gregory the great, who in that respect in the 20. bookes of his Morals, cap.23. termes that translation new. Neither doth he in all things follow it, for in his 1. book of Morals, c.19. he readeth not Ipsa conteres, but, Ipsa observabit. And after Gregories time, that alone was not received: for Bede, Gildas, and others, followed other translations now and then. And Bernard, Serm. in Cant. 24. readeth in Gen. 4. Sire tu eras, & non recte dividis, according to the Septuagints. It was not therefore only & wholly approoved of, for the space of a 1020 yeres after Christs; neither can it be shewed by any decree of the Church, that the Latine edition should bee held for authentical, before the late Councill of Trent.

8 It is probable that the vulgar translation which is made authenticall among the Catholikes, is not that which Hierom at Damasus his appointment did correct, for there are many errors in this, which Hierome did correct. The name of Esay in 1. cap v.2. of Marks Gospel, in the vulgar edition, Hierome thinkes was added by some copiers negligence, in Comment. in Mat. c.3. And upon the 6. chapt. of Mat. he corrected the word [exterminant] which the vulgar translation keepeth. And whereas the vulgar edition hath, Mat. 16. 23. vade post me, Hier. saith vade retro me. Againe in the epist. to the Galat. c.1. they say, Expugnabam illam: but he saith Comment. ibid. Devastabam illam: and in the same chapter they say acquievi, he, contuli. And upon the 3 chapter: It is written (quoth he) in certaine bookes, Quis vos fascinavit non credere veritati? but because this is not in Origens copy, we let it passe. In the 5 chapt the vulgar saith, Evacuati estis a Christo: he saith, a Christo opere cessastis, justly reprehending the former interpretation: yea Augustine himselfe, though he so greatly commend the translation of Hier. in his 10 epist. yet in more the 500 places he doth not follow this edition.

9 What the Fathers have spoken concerning the Churches allowance of the Scriptures, doth not belong to the Church that now is. That place of Augustine, Contra epist. fund. cap.5 [I would not beleeve the Gospel unlesse the authority of the Catholike Church moved mee] Gerson of Paris, lib. de vita spirituali lection. 2. Corolt holdeth not to be meant of any Church, but onely of the primitive Church which saw Christs person, or his Apostles, & could beare record of of their doctrine and writing. That which is spoken of the Churches approbation of the Scriptures, saith Durandus, lib. 3. dist.24. quaest.1. is meant of that Church only which was in the Apostles time, who were full of the holy Ghost, & besides saw Christs miracles, and heard his doctrine, and therefore were convenient witnesses of all things that he either did or said ——— so that the Gospels which that Church then received, cannot be by us now refused, because of the diversitie of the cases: whosoever thinketh otherwise, is an heretick, of what state, or condition so ever he bee.

What ground had Cusanus then for his assertion to the Bohemians, Epist. 2. viz. that the authority of the Scriptures doe depend upon the approbation of the present Church, and they have no more power to loose and binde, then the Church will give them. And that speech of Bellarmine is a foundation of Atheisme, If (quoth he De effectu sacram. lib.2.ca.25.) we should take away the authority and credit of this present Church and Councill of Trent, the Decrees of all other Councills, nay even Christian faith it selfe might bee called in question. Againe, the credit and certainty of all opinions and doctrines dependeth vpon the authority of the present church.

10 The Canonicall scripture is a principle of Divinitie deserving credit of it selfe, and therefore not manifestable by any other exteriour principle. The principles of Divinitie (saith Petrus de Alliaco in lib.1. Sentent. quaest.1. art.3.) are the very truths of the Sacred Canon. Moreover, the finall resolution of Theological discourse appertaineth unto them, and from them the conclusions of all Divinitie are drawne. Gods will (saith Ioachim Abbas in Apocalyps.) is, that wee acknowledging the letter of both the Testaments, presume not upon any other relation or opinion, further then the written word,

11 The holy Scriptures in all such things as are necessarie for our salvation doe manifestly, truly and infallibly explane and open themselves, serving for both gloss and text. The regular and diligent interpretation according to Scripture, (saith Irenaeus lib.4. cap.63. is without danger of errour, or blasphemie. Our teachings and allegations (saith Origen in Ierem. hom 1.) without these witnesses, the scriptures, have not any credit. And whereas it is said, In the mouthes of two or three witnesses shall every word stand, this rather belongs to the proofe of the interpreter, then to any certaine number of men whosoever: That I may confirme the word of my understanding, taking the two witnesses to be meant of the Old and new Testament, and the three to be spoken of the Gospell, the Prophet, and the Apostles; for so shall every word bee confirmed. The Scripture expounds it selfe (saith Chrysostome Hom. 13. in Genesin) and suffers not the hearer thereof to erre. So saith Augustine De doctr. Christ. lib.2. cap.6. and 16.17,18. and so Clement also, for you ought not (saith he, Epist.5. and he is cited dist.27.c. Relatum.) to seeke out any strange and impertinent sense, nor confirme it by confused allegations of the Scriptures, but fetch the truest sense indeed out of the scriptures themselves;

12 The infallible and determining judgment of all controversies of faith is in Christs owne person, or in the holy Ghost, so farre as hee speaketh unto us in the Scriptures canonicall. He, saith Tertullian De praescrip. sitteth at Gods right hand, but hee hath sent his deputie namely, the power of the holy Spirit to worke upon the hearts of the faithfull.

We must have judges sought out, saith Optatus contra Permenianum, but since earth affords no judgment of this matter, we must seeke a judge in heaven. But what need we knocke at heaven, since we have here a testament in the Gospell? An earthly father, feeling himselfe neere death, and fearing the contention of his sonnes after his death, calling some witnesses, hee transposeth his will out of his dying breast into lasting parchment. If so be now contention doe arise amongst the brethren, doe they runne to their fathers grave? no, but seeke out his will and testament, and he who sleepeth in his tombe speaketh lively out of the silent parchment. Hee whose this testament is, is in heaven; therefore his will is to be searched out in the Gospell as his testament. This Controversie, saith S. Augustine De nupt. & concupisc. lib.1. cap.33. requires a Iudge: then let Christ bee the Iudge, let him himselfe speake who it was that his death did profit: ——— And with him let the Apostle also judge, because in the Apostle Christ speaketh. And De grat. & lib. arbitr. cap.18. let the Apostle Iohn sit as a Iudge betweene us.

### Tradition.

1 The Fathers by the name of Tradition doe sometimes understand the doctrine received in the primitive Church, taught by the Apostles, and recorded in their writings. If it be taught in the Gospell, faith Cyprian Epist.74. ad Pompeium, or contained in the Epistles or Acts of the Apostles, that Converts from heresies should not bee baptized, but onely have imposition of hands, in signe of repentance; let this holy and Divine tradition bee observed.

2 They doe sometimes call that an unwritten tradition, which is contained onely in the sense of the Scriptures, and not in the words, and to this manner of speaking are referred all things gathered by analogy or proportion. Augustine faith De Genef. ad liter. l.10 cap.23. that Baptisme of children is an Apostolike tradition, yet De bapt. contra Donatist. cap.24. hee proves it out of the Scriptures. So holdeth he that denial of rebaptization unto heretikes is a tradition unwritten according to the words, but written in sense and foundation. Wherefore one and the same tradition may bee both written and unwritten: written in sense, unwritten in words.

Tradition is by Vincentius Lyrinensis used for the whole summe of Catholike doctrine, founded and grounded upon and in the scriptures: not containing any doctrine of faith without, or besides the scriptures, because he holds the scriptures the perfect and all sufficient rule for us that can bee; yea moreover he addeth, that the tradition of the Church is to bee followed onely in the chiefe questions, that are the foundations of the whole Christian faith and doctrine.

3 By the name of tradition are very often meant customes in things of liberty, or ecclesiastike rites; that is, rules concerning things and actions of comelinesse and government only, not pertinent any way to divine worship, or the articles of faith. And these for the more esteeme of order in the Church are called Apostolike, as the Grecian Idols for their more reverence were said to come down from Jupiter, Act.19. And Epicurus his booke de organo indicandi, was called [griego], that is, à Iove lapsus, fallen from Jupiter: and the porch in Ierusalem called Salomons after the common opinion, Iohn 10.23. whereas indeed, Herod built it. Every province, saith Hierome epist. ad Lucinium, thinketh their fathers precepts to be the Apostles doctrines. And in Agge. c.1. But the sword of God doth strike them for other things also, which they have invented and feigned of themselves, as Apostolike traditions, being without all allowance and testimonie of scriptures. And in Tertullian, tradition is taken for any custome of what originall soever. Dost thou not think, (saith he, De corona milit. ca.34. that it is lawfull for any Christian to invent and institute what doth agree with God, assist discipline, and helpe unto salvation?

The Fast of wednesday and friday is called an Apostolike tradition, Canon. Apost. 68. and Epiphan. haeref. 75. and yet we finde it seldome or never observed in the Catholike Church, which sheweth that it was Apostolike onely in name, and not indeed.

4 Some of the fathers inclining unto some heresies did make much of unwritten traditions. So doth Iustine Dial. cum Tryphone, defend the heresie of the Chiliasts by Apostolike tradition: so was Irenaeus deluded with traditions, for he held that Christ did live 50. yeares, which he saith he received by tradition from the Apostles. So Clement of Alexand. Stromat. lib.1. saith, that Gods workemen have a double husbandrie, written and unwritten: and no marvel, for this man will have the Gentiles saved by Philosophie. Irenaeus lib.3.cap.2. and Tertullian De praescriptione, doe both testifie that the old heretikes held the same opinion of Traditions, which neverthelesse they both doe confute. So dreamed Eusebius, de praepar. Evang. lib.1.cap.8. that the Apostles taught something in words, and other some in writings: and some things more excellent they reserved for the perfect only. Tertullian himselfe being fallen into Montanisme, gave himselfe over unto new prophecies and traditions.

5 The ancient Fathers speaking of these Traditions, doe oftentimes contradict themselves. So doth Basil. We preach (saith he,) l. de Spir. sanc. cap.27.) and observe some things out of the written word, and other some, which wee have received by mysticall tradition from the Apostles. And saith, that both these have like force and efficacie unto godlinesse. But Regul. moral. 8. and 26. epist. 80. he doth not sticke to say, that the Scriptures contained all things needfull to salvation.

So Chrysostome in 2. Thes. homil.1. It is a tradition, inquire no farther. But, in Psal. 95. homil.1. If we preach any thing without Scripture, our auditorie will be most uncertaine what to thinke, now assenting, now doubting, and sometimes plainly rejecting as frivolous the words they heare. Thus contrarieth he himselfe. And againe, Serm. de sancto & adorando Spir. If you heare any say, I have the holy Spirit, and yet he speake not out of the Gospell, but of his owne fantasie, he speaketh of himselfe, and the holy Ghost is not in him. And a little after, If any of those that are said to have the holy Ghost, doe speake aught besides the Gospell of themselves, beleeve them not, but follow my doctrine.

6 The Church now Romane doth not acknowledge the traditions which the ancient Fathers called Apostolike; and if it doe acknowledge them, yet it is not certaine that they are the Apostles. Thrice dipping in Baptisme is now out of use, talked of in Tertullian, de coron. mil. cap.3. and Basill, which also the 4. Councill of Toledo did disallow. Standing at prayers upon the Sundaies betweene Easter and Whitsontide now is quite forgotten, yet it was an old tradition. In Epiphan. by tradition no man may marrie after vow of singlenesse; and yet he alloweth those which burne, to marry, thinking it lesse evill to have one vice then many, though Papists now doe controule him, making a nullitie of such marriages. Neither use they now a daies to cause them newly-baptized to tast milke & hony, nor to cause the baptized of discretion to fast the weeke after their baptisme, nor to fast wednesday and friday, yee were all these Traditions. But let us heare Cassander minde heerein; There are thrie kindes of rites (saith he)[861] whereof the first is of such as were not of such moment as to binde unto the strict keeping of them: as those were in Tertullian and Hierome, of fasting milk and hony after baptisme, — as also not kneeling on the Lords day, nor upon all the 50. daies betweene Easter and Whitsontide, but praying standing: which old custome both held Apostolike, and instituted in the Councill of Nicaea, c.20. as also confirmed by the divine custome of the Churches: for all this hath no signe or token of the use thereof remaining amongus. For wee make no difference now betweene sunday and weekeday, onely upon some solemne fasts the Deacon exhorts us to kneele. Also the fast of wednesday & friday was once most religiously observed, which dayes Epiphan. saith, were by the Apostles appointed for holy assemblies. But this wednesday fast is now almost forgotten amongst the Romans, unlesse it be that some Provinces, and some private men doe upon this day abstaine from flesh. And the friday fast is changed into onely abstinence from flesh, as also almost the whole Lent: which abstinence doth but yeeld a vaine shew of the true and ancient fasting, since it brings unto many rather change of dainties, & greater excesse of luxury, then any restraint of bodily wantonnesse. Thus much Cassander.

Therefore the present Church of Rome can shew no consent of the catholike Doctors for those unwritten Traditions, which it hath set downe as necessary to salvation.
