[861] Defensio [ilegible] belli de offic. [ilegible] viri.

### The Mediatour.

1 The ancient Fathers do teach Christ to be the Mediatour (as hee is God & man) by a different act & operation, but in one and the same perfection proceeding from both the natures of Christ. For in his humane nature he wrought our salvation by suffering, dying, satisfying: and in his divine nature, by giving strength unto his humanitie to endure the death of the crosse, and perfect his satisfaction. The divine humanity (saith Augustine hom. de unitate c.12) & the humane divinity is our Mediatour. And in another place, de consensu Evang. l.1.c.35. Therefore is Christ called the Mediatour of God & man, betweene immortall God, and mortall man; God and man reconciling man unto God; remaining that which he was, & made that which he was not. Christs death (saith Cyril. l.1. de fide, ad Regin.) is confessed to be profitable unto us, but if he were not God, how could he, & he alone suffice for the price of all our redemption? but he onely in his death satisfied for all, because he is above all. Neither could wee bee freed (saith Augustine againe, Enchirid.cap.108.) by that one Mediatour of God and man; the man Christ, unlesse hee were God.

2 Whereas the ancient Fathers sometimes affirme, that Christ is Mediatour onely as he is man; & Mediatour, by that, by which he is man; and Mediatour in his humane nature, and Mediatour according to his manhood: they doe not speake of the manhood only and exclusively, but of the whole person, so considered as hee hath assumed mans nature and flesh upon him.

3 Whereas they deny Christ to be Mediatour as God, they speake of the godhead or of the Sonne of God absolutely considered, not of God as incarnate: that is, they speake of the bare Deitie, or of Christ as he is verbum Patris, the word of the Father. And there is not one of all the Fathers that saith, that Christ according to both his natures, is the Mediatour so, as his holy humanitie is the formall cause of his Mediatourship and the actions thereof: for the whole person compounded of God & man, according to both natures, is the beginning of all the operations of God-man.

Therefore it is a fiction of the Schoolemen to say, that Christ is the Mediatour onely according to his humanitie.

### The truth of the Humanity.

1 The ancient Fathers when they call Christs humanitie Deified, and Partaker of the Deitie, and supreme glory, in these and like phrases they expresse the personall Union; and they are to be understood with this caution, as farre as these things agree with the nature of the humanity, and do not infringe the properties thereof. Or, they speake thus in respect that the flesh is as the instrument of the Divinitie, by which and in which it doth exercise the power and actions thereof. The Lords flesh (saith Damascene, lib.3.cap.17.) is enriched with divine efficacy, because of the personall Union, neither yet doth it fall or depart from his owne proper nature, nor from the naturall properties thereof. And Nazianzene saith, Orat 41. that the humanity is endowed with divinity, and is God together with it: but this is in respect of the personall union, not essentially nor formally.

2 When the Fathers sometime say, that Gods omnipotencie is communicated unto the manhood of Christ, or to Christ as man, they must be expounded two waies: first, in respect that the man Christ is called omnipotent, because of the communication of the properties. Secondly, in respect that the proper workes of God are ascribed unto the flesh, as the Organ or instrument of the Divinitie; So doth Damascene, lib.3.cap.18. and Nicetas, Thesaur. lib.3. cap.38. use these sayings.

3 Some of the Fathers say, that Christs Nativity was without miracle, as other mens ordinarily are. So affirmes Ambrose upon the text Omne masculum aperiens vulvam, in Comment. in Luc. lib.2. and also Origen. Homil.14. in Luc. Tertullian in five lib. De carne Christi: Cyprian or Ruffinus, in Symbol. Apost. and Leo Epist. 84. & 97. is not farre from this opinion also. It is possible (saith Durandus, lib.4. dist.44. q.6.) that by the operation of the Deitie, there was made a dilatation or enlarging of the naturall parts and passages in the Virgin Mary, without any breach or interruption: And to confirme this, hee citeth Gregory upon the second of Luke. Againe Iesus came in when the doores were shut, but it is not said, that hee came through the doores being shut: ——— they might bee opened and shut againe in a moment, so as the Disciples might not perceive it.

4 The Fathers affirming the fulnesse of grace in Christ, doe meane of Christ as God, or of the whole person, nor of his soule. So meaneth Athanasius, in his 4. sermon against the Arrians, and Nazianzene in his Oration upon Basill.

5 The Fathers doe not with one consent affirme, that Christ had the fulnesse of knowledge from his conception, so as he could never have more. He received a soule (saith Origen, [griego] lib.4.) in nature and essence like unto one of ours. Therefore did Luke notifie his age (saith Ambrose, de Incarnat. Dom. cap.7.) because thou shouldest know that he spoke of his manhood: for it is the body, not the Deitie, that is the object of age. Wherefore, if he increased in the yeares of man, he also increased in the wisdome of man. Augustine is variable in this point, and yet that place of Luke, Puerulus crescebat — hee held to bee meant of Christs humanitie, De Genef. ad liter. lib.10. c.18. Growing up in age and wisdome (saith Bruno Herbipolensis, in Symb. Apost.) after his holy nativitie, hee came to the age of thirtie yeares.

6 That which the Fathers doe attribute unto the name of Iesus, or of Christ, is not properly ascribed to the bare name, but as it is invocated by men, or to the invocation of the name; often times I have scarce pronounced that name (saith Nazianzene, ad Nemesium,) when the divell presently halted away. The divels gave place (saith Origen, contra Celf. lib.1.) at the very calling upon the name of Iesus. And lib.3. the sicke were cured by calling upon the Almightie God, and the name of Iesus over them. Hilarion (saith Hierome, in vita Hilari.) cast out divels by invocating the name of Iesus.

### The descension into hell, (to deliver the Fathers.)

1 The Fathers doe sometimes defend a vertuall descension of Christ into hell and a vertuall deliverance from hell, that is, by the merit and vertue of his passion and death, not a local. This Augustine (in Psal.85.) doth acknowledge. And Durandus, lib.3.Sent. dist.22. quaest.3. denieth any other descension of Christ into the place of the damned, then one vertuall, or in the effect. Thomas also (par.3. quaest.52. artic.2.) denies that Christ was really in any other place save Limbo, but in the place of the damned onely vertually, or in effect. In this sense many testimonies of the Fathers must be taken figuratively. In like manner they say that Adam and others were in hell, not locally, but according to their desert, yea and that before they died.

2 Those of the Fathers that defend a local descension and deliverance, doe not defend it as an article of the Creede, but as a probable opinion. This may bee proved, because they seldome or never put this Article into their creeds and confessions of the faith. You must know (saith Ruffinus, in expos. Symbol.) that in the Church of Rome, this article, hee descended into hell, is not put in the creed, nor in the creed of the Easterne Church, though it seeme to bee included in these words, dead and buried. Nay this Article is not in any creed or confession almost of all the Fathers. It is not in Marcellus his confession in Epiphanius, not in Ignatius his confession, in ep.ad Magnetianos, vel ad Ephesios: not in that of Polycarp, (Epist.ad Philippenses.) not in Iustinus, (in Apolog.1.) nor in Irenaeus his, (lib.1.cap.2.) not in Tertullian, lib. de Praescript. vel contra Praxeam, though hee explane the Apostles Creed: not in Origens, in Proemio [griego] where he intreates of faith: not in Gregories of Neocaesaria: nor in the Councills of Nicaea, Socrat.lib.1.cap.5. not in Eusebius his creed of Caesaria, (Theodoret. lib.1.cap.12.) not in the third creed rehearsed in the Nicene Councill, Socrat.lib.1.cap.5. not in Athanasius his creed. Epist.ad Epictetum. not in that creed which is in Athanasius his epistle touching the Councils of Arimin and Seleucia; not in the Synod of Syrmias creed, Socrat.lib.2.cap.25. Hilar.lib.de Synod. contr. Arian. not in the Councill of Sardica's creed, Theodoret.lib.2.cap.8. not in Hilaries exposition thereof; not in the creed of the Synod of Antioch, set downe by Hilary, lib. de Synod. contra Arian. not in the creed of Seleucia a citie of Isauria, in Socrates, lib.2.cap.31. Epiph. haeref.73. not in the Synod of Illyria, Theodoret.lib.4.8. not in Damasus his creed, set downe by Hierome, Tom.2.operum. Theodoret. lib.5.chapter 10. not in Eusebius Pamphilus his creed, Socrat.lib.1.cap.5. not in Hilaries de Synodis cont. Arianos: not in Basils creed, in his Ascetica. not in Nazianzene; nor in that of Victorinus, l.1.contr. Arian. nor in Epiphanius his Ancoratum: where the Catholike faith is rehearsed, not in Theodoret, in Dialog. Impatibilis, where the Nicene creed is expounded: nor in Maximus Taurinensis, where he expounds the creed: nor in that which Chrysologus repeateth foure times, Homil.56,57,58. not in that of the first Councill of Toledo, nor in the Ephesine creed, Anno 435. not in that of the first Councill of Constant. not in that of the 6. councill of Constant. Act.10. Not in that of the Synod of Chalcedon, in Zonaras: not in the Creed of the Fathers in Cyril, ad Reginam, l.2. not in that of the third Councill of Toledo, nor in that of Gregory the fift, not in Spiridions. Nicephorus lib.8. cap.15. nor in that which then Bishops of the East offered Confirmis, Nicephorus lib.9. cap.11. nor in that whiche the Legats of the West offered: the same Emperour, Nicephorus lib.18. cap.10. nor in the booke of faith upon Petrus Diaconus, nor in Augustine, wherein if ever he expounds the Creed, although in his workes; lib. de fide & Symb. In libris 4. de fid. ad Catechumen. Serm. de tempore 123.125. here doth explane it five severall times: nor in the first exposition of the Creed, in Chrysostomes Sermone.

3 The Fathers by Christs descension into hell, do sometime understand his descending into the lower parts of the world, Christ not onely in his death, but also in his birth, saith Bede Psal.95; die descend into hell. And in the 6. generall Councill. Act. 10. is left out, He descended into hell, and there is put in, He descended out of heaven. And so it is also in the Nicene Councill. Ibid. Act. 17. And in the Ephesine Creed, He descended from the heavens. In the 6. and 11. of Toledo, it is, Being sent from his Father hee came into the world.

4 The descension into hell sometimes, is put for buriall. As in Athanasius his creed, and the latter exposition of the creed in Chrysostome. And in the creed of Toledo 4. there are these words, Hee descended into hell to free the Saints there captive, and having overcome the dominion of death, hee rose againe. And in Hierome, in Proem. comment. in Esay. Being buried, and rising againe — he is preached. He descended not onely into hell (saith Radulphus Ardens) In vigil. ascen. hom. 2. but also into the lower parts of the earth, that is, into the place of torment, breaking it up, and leading away captivitie captive.

5 The Fathers either knew not at all, or (if they knew) yet speake doubtfully of the severall places of hell: and therefore sometimes oppugne Limbus Patrum which is called a part of hell: and some times (but uncertainly) make for it. Abrahams bosome (saith Augustine epist.99.) that is, the habitation of secret rest, is not to be held any part of hell. And De remissione peccatorum, lib.1. cap.28. There is no middle place for any man to be (saith he) but with the devill, that is not with Christ. Although (saith he De Genesi ad literam, lib.12. cap.33.) I confesse I have not yet found that the place where the righteous rested (as Abrahams and Lazarus) is called hell: neither where they are said to bee in hell, have I yet found, but I still doe seeke, and know not. Nor doe I finde in all the scriptures (which are Canonicall) that hell is taken in good part or sense, and therefore I cannot see how Abraham can bee said or beleeved to bee in hell. Againe, Perhaps (saith hee In Psal.85.) there is a lower part of hell where the sinners are, which were very wicked, for whither Abraham was in any of those places, who cannot certainly be determined. And againe, Perhaps hee meanes these two hels, &c. Tertullian, will haue Abrahams bosome (wherein he thinkes the just soules and till the last judgement from hell. Hell is one place, (saith he Contra Marcion lib.4. cap.31.) and Abrahams bosome another. And I call that region Abrahams bosome, which if it be not heavenly, yet is higher then hell, giving rest unto the soules of the righteous, untill the consummation of all things doe terminate their resurrection, with the fulnesse of blessednesse. Here also hee ascribeth this opinion of Lubus unto Marcion: Marcion (saith he) thinketh otherwise, namely, hee determineth both the rewards of the creator, whither it be of torment, or rest, in hell, unto those that kept or breake the law and the prophets, but heaven unto Christ, and to his God. And in I. De anima cap.7. What is that which is transported unto hell after the separation from the body, and unto what did Christ descend in his death? I thinke, unto the soules of the Patriarkes. Concerning the first man (saith Augustine epist.99.) and our first parent, the whole church almost doth agree in this, that Christ freed him from thence; which we must thinke was not beleeved upon the ground, whencesoever it first came up, although wee haue no authority of Canonicall Scripture to authorize it at all. These perhaps (saith Iulian of Toledo, Prognost. lib.2. cap.4.) were the two hels, in one whereof the soules of the just were at rest, and in the other the wicked punished. Bede in Psal.85. (saith he) that the earth is the Upper hell, and that the place of punishment after this life, is the lower hell.

6 Of the intent of Christ in his descension, the Fathers speake variably, and must hold that he went to free the soules of the Saints out of the bonds and captivitie of death. I thinke it no absurditie (saith Augustine De civit. Dei lib.20. cap.15.) to beleeve, that the Saints of old that expected Christ in faith, were in habitacles farre distant from the tormentes of the wicked, but yet did they say they were in hell, untill that Christs blood and descending thither set them free. But in epist.99. more plainly, I do not finde (saith he) what good Christ did unto those just ones that were in Abrahams bosome, by his descending into hell, from whom according to the blessed presence of his Divinity, hee was never absent. Christ descended into hell (saith Clement of Alexandria) most plainly Stromat.6. for no other cause but to preach the Gospell to the Gentiles, that they might learne the truth faith and beleeved, or justly bee condemned forever. And thus also Damascene in Oratione de fidelibus defunctis holdeth. But this opinion is condemned by Philaster cap.74. There are heretikes (quoth hee) that say that Christ descended into hell, and there after his death told them all, that who so there confessed him should be saved. Looke Augustine De haeref.cap.79. concerning this, and Gregory lib.6. indict.15. epist.15. Christ descended into hell for us sinners, saith Fulgentius and Thrasimund lib.3. cap.31. Christ descended saith Epiph. Haer.46 contra Tatianos, to give pardon unto those that erred not from acknowledging his deity, but were kept in hell for other errors: yea Bellarmine himselfe De anima Christi lib.4. cap.15. confesseth, that this in the beliefe of Christs descension is not of necessity, but of decency or conformity. Although (quoth hee) it bee not necessarie that Christs soule should be present in the illumination of the fathers with divine vision: yet it seemes fit that it should bee present while that was doing. But the articles of our faith (good M. Bellarmine) bee founded upon somewhat besides congruitie, they stand upon necessity.

7 Those that will haue the Fathers in hell untill Christs ascension, doe contradict themselves, or one another. 1. Some, as Ruffinus for one, will haue them in paines. The King (saith he In expos. Symbol.) was said to be in prison also, but not as the rest were: they were there to suffer paines, but hee to release them. Athanasius: De salutar. Christi advent, saith, Adams soule and the rest that served God in the law of nature, were in sorrow, and cried out. By Christ, saith Anastasius Sinaites, in Hexamer. was Adam freed from his sorrowes. And De resurrectione fidei dogmat. lib.5. The soules were freed out of the cloisters of hell where they were holden in most miserable tyranny, perhaps not tyranny, yet guilty of the debt of a multitude of sinnes. Presently upon Christ descension (saith Caesarius Homil.3. de Paschate,) that eternall night of hell had morning: the noise of the mourners was silent, the huge weights of the chaines were laid off, and the bands of the damned fell away all broken.

2 Other some will haue them in a quiet repose without all molestation. So will Hierome haue them, Ad Paulam epist.25. cap.3. and Augustine De genes. ad lit. lib.12. cap.33. So that Abraham, although hee was in that place of repose, yet is said to haue beene in hell with Lazarus.

### Free-will.

1 Some of the Fathers speaking of Free-will, and in some places doe meane of the freedome which was in our nature before our fall: or of the freedome of glorie. So meaneth August. Hypognost.3. (or whosoever was the author of that booke) when hee saith, unto Adam was that spoken, Eccles.15. If thou wilt keepe thy commandements they shall keepe thee.

2 Other some things are spoken of the naturall freedome of our will from necessity, from which it cannot but be free. And in this sense they say, that we haue a will absolutely free in all things, that is, an understanding minde, and will whereby we assent unto or dissent from our judgement, by which also which we doe, we doe it wittingly & willingly, not compelled. Gregory Arim.lib.2.dist.25. in fine, saith, It is sufficient to make a thing voluntary, if it be done by him that knoweth and is willing. The soule hath freewill, saith Cyrill Catech.4. the devill may stirre it up unto sinne, but constraine it against the will, cannot. God made us of a free consent, saith Hierome, in Jovinian.lib.4. neither are we forced by necessity either to vertue or vice. And these speake of the libertie wee haue in reasonable and sensible things; So doth Augustine de perfect.justit.contra Caelestium, and Caelestius, objecting that of Saint Paul, faciat quod vult, As though (saith he) it were a great matter to desire to wedde, where the disputation is earnest concerning the assistance of Gods mercy. Neither let a man thinke, saith the Author in Ambroses words, De vocat. Gent. lib.1.cap.3. because hee is drawne on by the Spirit of God, that he hath not free-will, for he lost not that when he yeelded himselfe in will unto the devill, by whom indeed the judgement of his will was depraved, but not utterly taken away. So saith Euthymius, in Luc.15. cap. of the prodigall sonne: He asked that part of the goods which fell unto him, that is, freewill, as if hee should say, urge me not necessarily to serve, for I haue free-will. So Bernard, De grat. et lib. arbit. saith, Seeing then that consummation or perfection in glorie must be wrought upon us or even in us, but not of our selves; and that our creation was wrought, and that without us, there is onely reformation, which after a sort is wrought with us by reason of our voluntary consent, that shall be reckoned to our desert.

3 Some things also are spoken of free-will as of a good belonging to naturall life, or an externall morall good, or of outward discipline. And this manner of speaking the author of the booke in Augustine called Hypognosticon useth, lib.3. He is rightly said to be but halfe alive, saith he, for he had his vitall motion, that is, his freewill wounded. And so Gregorie of Arimin.2. dist.26. and after him Cassalius de quadripartita Institutione lib.1. doe speake of goodnesse considered in the kind, object, and office; not of good from all circumstances.

4 Some of their sayings hereof are legall, in that they shew, not what wee can doe, but what we cannot doe through sinne, and what we ought to doe in duty. The Pelagians (saith Augustine, De grat. & lib. arbit.cap.16.) thinke themselves great scholars, when they object that God would not command what hee knoweth impossible to bee kept; who knoweth not that? but therefore hee commands us some things which we cannot doe, because we shold know what we ought to beg of him

5 Other some are meant of the will being freed, and therefore shew what our will may doe in a worke truly good not of it selfe, and it owne naturall power, but what it can do by grace.

6 Most of the Fathers correct their owne vnfit speeches of free will, (but chiefly Augustine.) For indeed almost all of them speake contraries, that none can tell their positive doctrines: sometime they extoll humane power too much, and that first because if they should directly haue affirmed the weakenesse of the will, the Philosophers might haue scorned them. 2. Because they would not giue the reines vnto negligence. And sometimes they beate downe the liberty of will on the other side. Chrysostome doth often giue too much to the power of the will after the fall: and yet sometimes correct himselfe. A man before hee sinneth, (saith hee, Serm. 1. de Adventu.) hath Free-will, to choose whether hee will yeeld to the divell, or no: but when hee hath once taken that subjection vpon him by sinne, then hee is no more at his owne command. Thou hast nothing (saith Basil, Serm. de humilit.) left thee oh man, to bee proud of; whose glory and hope should be to mortifie all thine owne affections, & seeke the life to come in Christ: whose first fruites we hauing reaped, do owe our life, and all we are, vnto the gift and grace of God. For it is hee that giueth vs both to will and to doe according to his good pleasure.

7 The Fathers before Pelagius, while the controversies of Free-wil were not stirred vp, spake thereof very securely, like as Pelagius did, chiefly, they that opposed the Marcionists, Valentinians, or the Manichees: with whom whilest they contend about the heresie of the necessity of all things, and of all events, they misse the way a little, in giuing too much to Free-will, and too little vnto grace, at least in shew. There were nought of any worth in man, (saith Iustine, Apolog.1.) vnlesse hee had an equall power to turne vnto what part hee list. God doth not force any (saith Irenaeus, lib.4. capite 71.) but is alwaies well meaning, and therefore hee counselleth all men vnto good. But hee hath giuen man a free election euen as well as the angels. We are all of one nature (saith the same Father, capite 72.) able to keepe good, and so to worke, and able to lose good, and not to worke in it. There should no law haue beene giuen, (saith Tertullian Contra Marcion. libro 2.) vnto him that hath not the due keeping of the law in his owne power——: and the same freedome of will (which was in Adam) maketh vs victors of the same devill.

It is our parts to beginne, (saith Hierome Contra Pelagium, libro 1. capite 1.) & Gods to perfect: wee must doe what wee can, hee will fulfill what we cannot. Vnlesse the Patriarke (saith Chrysostome, in Genef. homil 41.) had first done his part, hee had not obtained so great things of God: and therefore marke not onely this, but in all things else; how first hee sheweth the greatnesse of his vertue, and so thereby deserues Gods assistance. And againe: (homil. 17. in Ioan.) let vs here observe, that God in his blessings to vs, doth not prevent our wils, but it must beginne in our selves; and when hee seeth our mindes prompt and ready to receiue grace, then hee giueth vs many occasions of salvation. I said, (saith Austen, de praedest. Sanct. libro primo, capite tertio) that it lieth in vs to beleeve and to will; and in God to giue the power of working well; vnto the beleeving and willing. To propound or begin a good worke (saith Hesychius in Levit. libro 2. capite 7.) is in our power: but to perfect and finish it according to the precept, is onely in Gods grace. After Pelagius was risen vp, Cassianus held with him concerning Free-will: (as Prosper saith of him, contra Collatorem) for in one of his Collations, Collatio 13. cap. 11. hee affirmeth, that the grace of God sometime preventeth vs, and sometimes is prevented by vs. So held Faustus Rhegiensis.

8 Augustine after Pelagius was risen, in all his last writings, neuer acknowledgeth either the exercise, or the actiue power of Free-will in working true good, or in the first conuersion of a sinner. Why doe wee presume so much, saith hee, (De natura & grat. capite 35.) of the power of nature? it is wounded, maimed, vexed, and lost: let vs confesse it freely, and not defend it falsly: Wherefore let vs seeke the grace of God, not to informe, but to reforme it thereby. And in the Hypognost. 3. cap. primo, it is said, that by sinne man did lose both the abilitie of goodnesse, and the goodnesse of possibilitie. The will (saith Augustine in another place, De perfect.iustit.) beeing ouercome by sinne, hath lost her libertie. And againe, de spirit. & lit. capite tertio. Free-will hath not any power but vnto sinne, if the way of truth bee vnknowne: and when that which is to bee done beginneth to appeare, vnlesse also it doth delight, and bee beloved, there is no doing, no vndertaking, no well liuing. Wee are therefore willing, but God is hee that worketh this willingnesse in vs; and wee worke, but God giueth vs this ability to worke according vnto his good pleasure, Augustine, De bono perseuerantia, capite 13. It is certaine, that wee are willing when wee are so; but it is hee that makech vs so, of whom it is said: It is God that worketh this will in vs. It is certaine that wee worke when wee doe so; but it is hee that giueth vs this working power, by giuing our will most efficient power, as if hee said, I will cause you worke, Augustine, De grat. & lib. arbit. capite 16. Vnlesse hee first worke vs to bee willing, & then worke with vs being willing, we shall neuer bring to passe any good worke.

Wee must confesse, that wee haue Free-will both to good and euill: but in doing euill euery man iust and vniust is free (in choice:) but in doing good, none can bee free (in will and act) vnlesse hee bee freed by him that said: If the Sonne free you, you are truly freed, Augustine de corrept. & grat. capite primo. Holy thoughts, good purposes, godly counsels, and all motions of a good will are from God: because by him wee are able to do some good, without whom wee can doe nothing at all, Author de dog. Eccles. cap.17. Wee lost our free election to loue God, by the greatnesse of the first sin, Epist. 107. Libertie without grace is no liberty, but contumacy, Idem, Epistol.89. ad Hilar. Man in his creation had great power of free-will giuen him, but in his fall he lost it. Idem de verb. Apost. Serm.2. And you shall very often finde these words in Augustine. Our bound will, captiued, destroyed, lost, &c. Of this opinion of Augustine, was Prosper also. Infidelitie (saith he, contra Collatorem, capite 21.) tooke away our faith, bondage tooke away our libertie; neither can any part of vertue remaine there, where such a crue of vices haue broke in. Adam (saith Fulgentius de Incarn. & gra. cap.13.) being created without necessity of sinning, when he lost his soules health in offending God, lost utterly even the power of thinking of all divine things. Againe, in another place, cap.13. The power of thinking good thoughts, being lost in the first man, was recovered in the second. We beleeve (saith Maxentius, de Fide, capite 32.) that our free naturall will, hath power in nothing, but in discerning & desiring worldly and carnall things onely, which seeme not glorious before God, though before men perhaps they doe. But in things belonging to salvation, it can neither thinke of them, choose, desire, nor finish them without the infusion and operation of the Spirit of God. And hee addeth: To will and to performe is Gods gift. Bernard teacheth, that it is one thing to choose, and another to choose good: To will (quoth he, de grat. & libero arbit.) is in vs by Free-will, but not to performe our will; I say not, to will either good or evill, but onely to will: for to will good, is increase, (of grace hee meaneth,) and to will evill, is defect. Free-will maketh vs willing, but grace maketh vs well-willing: from free-will we haue power to will: but to will well comes from grace.

9 Augustine in divers places plainly affirmeth all the workes of the unfaithfull to bee sinnes, De nupt. & concup. libro primo, capite tertio, In Iulii libro 4. capite 3. De ciuit. Dei libro 5. capite 19. & libro 19. capite 25. in Psal.31. In praefat. Our Freewill saith hee, contr. Iulian. Epist. Pelag. libro 3. capite 8. beeing now captiuated can do nothing but sinne. So Hierome in Galat. capite 3. Without Christ all vertue is vice. And Gregorie very rightly, Moral. libro 2. capite 33. The sonnes doe feast in the elder brothers house, when all other vertues are entertained in faith, which if it be not the first begotten in our heart, all the rest can neuer bee good, though they seeme neuer so well. It is through the gift of God, whensoeuer wee decline from sinne, saith the Councell of Arausic: But Stapleton, De iustific. libro 2. capite vltimo, scourgeth this doctrine, and stickes not to surmize, that Augustine went a little beyond his bounds in this Controversie with Pelagius. But other moderne writers holding with Augustine, doe flatly deny, that a man by the power of nature can discerne or distinguish of a morall good. So holdeth Gregory of Arimin. in 2. dist. 26. quaest. 1. art. 2. & in 2. dist. 28. quaest. 1. art. 3. Cassalius de quadrip. institut. lib.1. capite 15. & 32. &c. Also these deny, that a man without faith, and the especiall helpe thereof, by natures power can doe a good morall worke; so as there be no sinne in the action or worke. Both Gregory of Ariminium, and Capreolus in 2 dist. 28. hold this: But Cassalius de quadrip. institut. lib.1. cap.36. both teacheth and defendeth, that the Fathers were of this minde. This also is Marsilius his opinion, in 1 quaest. 20. Bellarmine indeed confesseth, that Scotus, Durandus, and Biel (upon the 28. Distinction of Lumbards second booke) haue perhaps written more freely then is behoovefull. Sixtus Senensis saith, Praefat. in libro 5. Biblioth. that Augustine sometimes gives but too little unto mans Free-will: and Chrysostome on the contrary seemes to extoll it as much beyond the meane;[862] Bradwardine in his booke De causa Dei, against Pelagius, libro 3. capite 4. teacheth that Freewill being tempted, cannot overcome any temptation by it selfe, without the assistance and grace of God.[863] And this also in another place, capite 5. ibid. With what grace of the creation soever it be up-held, yet without some speciall grace of God, it cannot conquer any temptation at all. And againe, c.6 ibid. That that speciall helpe of God, is Gods invincible will.

10 The Fathers say, that our will is assisted by God, according as we sometimes say, Such a man helped me to doe this, when as hee did all, and nothing.

11 The Fathers hold a possibilitie of turning, wherby mans mind & will may by Gods ordinary dispensation, be turned to receiue grace, when they are preuented and helped by the holy Spirit. To be able to haue faith and charity, (saith Austen, de praedest. Sanct. c.5.) is in mans nature. And againe, contra Iulian. l.2. Mans nature is capable of justification by the grace of the holy Spirit. Gregory of Arimin. vnto that of Augustine: [There is nothing so much in mans power as to will,] saith thus, lib.2. dist.28. We may say, that it is in our power not onely to will or choose bad things, but also good things; but with this difference, we may vse our election vnto evill without Gods especiall helpe: but unto good, if he doe not chiefly assist us, we cannot. It is in mans power, saith Augustine, Retract. lib.1. cap.22. to change his bad will into better, but this power is none at all untill God give it. And ibid. cap.23. We may will to beleeve, it is true; but with the same condition: they are both from him (viz. to will and to beleeve) because hee prepareth our will: and both from us, because they bee not done against our wils. And in this sense are many sayings of S. Augustine to be understood. For he speaketh of the passive possibilitie, which belongs to the matter, not of the active, belonging to the forme, which is absent before the conversion, both according to the first and second act.

12. The Fathers acknowledge a co-operation with the Grace of God, even naturall, in respect of the faculties of the understanding and will: and also from the grace of God, in respect of willing that which is good. Hee that made thee without thy selfe, saith Augustine, De verb. Apost. Serm.15. doth not justifie thee without thy selfe. And hee that made thee not witting, doth justifie thee being willing, and without thy will there shall no righteousnesse be in thee. Therefore the Papists doctrine of Free-will, that it is but halfe dead, that is, bound from use or exercise, but not dead in respect of the active power of willing well, is not Catholike.

[862] Hem[ilegible] bishop[ilegible] terbury, 1550.

### Of the Remainders of Concupiscence.

1 Whereas sometime in the Fathers wee finde it written, that Concupiscence is no sinne after regeneration, it must be thus understood, because that God of his mercy doth not impute it. So that the Fathers doe onely deny that concupiscence is sinne unto the person in whom it is; but, that it is sinne in it selfe and of it selfe, and so remaineth after baptisme, they never denie, but doe averre it so to bee. Augustine himselfe, Contr. Iul. Pelag. lib.5. cap.3. very plainely calleth that concupiscence sinne, against which the good spirit doth strive, because, saith hee, there is in it a disobedience against the rule of the minde. And againe, De nupt. & concup. lib.1. cap.26. This is to bee free from sinne (saith he) not to be guilty of sinne. Besides, Tractat. In Ioan 41. Let not sinne rule the lust, let it not be in thee, for as long as thou liv'st, thou art sure to have sinne in thy members, but yet let it not rule in them. So Ambrose, apud Aug. contra Iul.2. c.5. calleth the remains of concupiscence in the regenerate, iniquity, and Hilary calleth it materiam malitiae, apud eundem, lib.2. cap.8. Caietane, in Rom. capite 7. verse 8. sticks not to say that concupiscence (whereof Saint Paul speaketh) is even formally sinne, in respect that it is a part of originall sinne.

2 The first motions of concupiscence, before consent, the Fathers hold to bee sinne. So holdeth Bede: Carnall concupiscences saith he, in Psal.9. are the first death, & deaths entry. And in Psal.114. Whosoever falls but in thought, offendeth God: and againe, In Psal.1. The soule is killed three waies; with delectation alone, with delight joyned with consent, and with action. Sure, saith Radulphus, In Leviticus lib.3. cap.4. doth breede in a mans soule before consent, and now beginneth to be brought forth, but is not consummate or perfected. And Cassiodorus, In Psalm.119. calleth those desires unlawfull, to which wee doe not consent: and Augustine also before him, in Psalm.118. Conc.3. doth the like.

3 When the Fathers say, that the first motions in concupiscence are not sinnes, unlesse we consent, we must not so understand them; as though they were not sinnes in the truth of appellation, but because the guilt of these first motions, together with the guilt of concupiscence it selfe, is taken away in our regeneration: So saith Augustine, De peccat. origin. lib.2. cap.40. The vicious desires also (unto which if we doe not consent, there is not guilt contracted) are all purged away in the same fountaine of regeneration. And againe, Contra Iul. lib.2. cap.10. As for us, we should be alwaies without sinne, if this evill were once cured; and if we should never consent with it unto evill. But hee had said before, sup. 9. in fine. How then doe we say, that this sinne is dead in baptisme, and yet confesse that it dwelleth still in our members, and causes many desires in us against our wils, unto which we resist by not consenting. Unlesse because it is dead touching that guilt, wherewith it held us: and yet untill it bee cured in the consummation of buriall, a will-rebell though it bee dead, although now it is not called sinne, after the same manner whereby it maketh a man guilty, but in that it was caused by the guilt of the first man Adam, and by rebellious nature endeavours to bring us into guilt, unlesse we be helped by Gods grace, through Iesus Christ. Looke his third sermon in Psal.118. Hence it is that Augustine saith often, that wee need not say, forgive us our trespasses, for the unvoluntary motions of our concupiscence, because hee held them all forgiven in baptisme, epist.200. ad Asselec. libro de perfect. justit. in Psal.118. conc.3.

4 Sometimes they speake of the externall suggestions of Sathan; and those indeede are no sinnes of ours, unlesse wee give our assent unto them, so saith Gregory, Moral. libro 21. cap.3.

### Veniall sinne.

1 A Veniall sinne which is besides Gods Law, and not against it, and in his nature bindeth onely unto the guilt of temporall punishment, was not knowne among the Fathers for seaven hundred yeares after Christ: Afterwards it got entrance and patronage. The reward, saith Haimo, In epist. dominica 8. post pentecosten, of sinne is death: not of all sinnes, but onely of those that are criminall, and whereof Iohn saith, It is a sinne unto death.

2 The Fathers acknowledge, that all sinne properly, and of it owne nature, deserveth eternall death by the just judgement of God. There is a daily repentance of good & humble beleevers, saith August. epist. 108. when knocking our breasts wee say, forgive us our trespasses,—for we do not begge forgivenes for those which we know are forgiven in baptisme: but for them which (though but sinne all,) yet are often incident unto humane frailtie; and beeing drawne to a summe against us, would oppresse us as much as another heavy sinne: for what difference is it in shipwracke to be sunke with one furious billow, or to have the water enter by little and little, and never respect it untill it sinke the shippe? And againe, Tract. 12. in Ioan. many little, or small sinnes unregarded, kill the soule. Besides: Expos. 1 in epist. Ioan. many light sinnes make one heavie one. All sinne (saith Nazianzen, Orat. 31.) is the death of the soule. And who is he, saith the author Asteriscum, that dare say this sinne is little, what euer it be? I know not, saith Hieron. epistol.14. how we can call any sinne light, which is done in contempt of God. The reprooving sentence of the severe judge, saith Bede, In Samuel, libro prim. cap. 10. doth not onely condemne those fires of capitall sinnes, wherein the devill his workes are manifest; but even all little ones, and these also which men may hold slender or light. Every sinne saith Gregorie, In Ezec. lib 1 hom. 2. is heavy, because it withholdes the soule from ascending. To use idle speeches, saith Sixtus 3. De malis dictis & opera, or to call a man a foole, seeme small and slender faults: but he addeth, If he be guilty of hell that doth but call his brother foole; what sin can then be nor deserving hel, I leave the reader to judge. All sin, saith Gr. Ion. De vitae spirit. dist. 8. in that it is an offence to God, against his eternall Law, is in his own nature and indignitie, deadly, according to the rigour of justice, and severing a man from the life of glorie. Againe. No offence is veniall in it selfe, but onely through Gods mercy, who will not impute all offences expresly unto death, when as in justice hee might so that it is accounted, that sinne mortall, and veniall in being so, are not intrinsecally and essentially distinguished, but onely in respect of the divine mercie, which imputeth the one unto death, and not the other; and thus holdeth Roffensis, In refut. articul. 32 Lutheri. That opinion, saith Bajus, professour of Louaine, is not to be reproved, which saith, that even light sinnes, excluding Christs blood, in their own nature, barre us from heaven; this he proves by many texts of Scripture.

3 The Fathers call sinne veniall, not because it is so in it selfe, but because it is in the person of the righteous, unto whom is given remission of sinne in Christ, through the grace of God. In this sense Bede, comment. in 1. Iohan. 5. saith: There are some small sinnes, which cannot take from the just, the merit of their justice, nor diminish it. Sin, saith Cyril, Catec. 2. is heavy to the retainer, and light to the rejecter: and Cassianus, Collat. 22. saith, that such sinnes are pardonable unto the righteous.

4 Also that was called a veniall sin, which had pardon in the censure of the Church: for greater sinnes were thought worthy excommunication, and for those was publike penance performed; but in these lighter, that is, veniall sinnes, it was not so; and hereupon is veniall, so often opposed unto criminall. There are some sinnes great and pernicious saith Tertullian, de pudicitia, and other some that we daily runne into, and to which wee are so incident, that if they were not pardonable, no man could bee saved, but for these there is pardon in Christ the Mediatour. So August. epistol. 89. saith, There are some vices called crimes, and some, without which no man liveth. And Cesarius, Homil. 1. sinne is either capitall, or small: Capitall, as murder, sacriledge, &c. And Bede in Psal. 3. opposeth veniall sinne unto criminall, taking criminall for that which the magistrate punisheth. Now this that the Fathers speake of sinnes after the manner and respect of men, the Schoole-men have transferred unto God, and so have set downe a kinde of sinne which needeth not Christs blood to purge it.

5 Thirdly, that is called a Veniall sinne, which obtaineth pardon in the event & consequent, though it be morrall in it selfe. So Ambrose, lib. de parad. cap.4. That fault is pardonable, which a confession of sinnes doth follow. There are some sinnes (saith the author, de vera & falsa poenit. apud Aug. cap. 18.) that are in themselves mortall, but by repentance are made veniall. Now (saith August. de Civit. Dei, l. 21. c. 27,) since wee know not the measure of our veniall iniquitie (though it be little in us) surely we take greater paines to profit in good, and bee more fervent in prayer. And the mortall sinne hereunto opposed, is the sinne that leadeth unto death, so saith Pacianus epist. 3. ad Sempronium, and Hieron. in Jerem. capite 2. calleth those heavie sinnes, which draw man to destruction, and opposeth lighter sinnes thereto. So the author of the prayers in Prudentius at the end of his Hamartigenia, saith: [ilegible] upon judging still, Of all my sinnes for pardon hope I will, Although my words and deedes be mere ill.

6 Fourthly, sinne is called veniall, because it is excusable before men, through humane goodwill: so an officious lie is veniall: And August. Enchir. cap. 22. saith: Therefore it is a sinne, but veniall, which benevolence excuseth. And they are called veniall respectively, in reverence to greater crimes: So Cassianus Collat. 22. saith of veniall sinnes, they seeme light and small unto men: and Sixtus 3. de malis dictis & operi. fidei, they seeme little and slender, and are esteemed light: and this is in respect of the greater.

### Images and Reliques.

1 There was no use of images receiued at all in the primitiue Church, but onely Symbolicall, and for ornament sake, and that in priuate places, for 380. yeares after Christ. Irenaeus objected against the Gnosticks, lib. 1. c. 24. that first they had the image of Christ painted, then that they crowned it, and worshipped it. Looke also Augustine de haeres. 7. and Epiphanius, in haeres. 27. We worshippe no images, saith Origen, Contra Celf. libro 7. for wee doe not binde our invisible and incorporall God unto any figure. So Arnobius, or rather Minutius Felix contra Gent. libro 8. What image shall wee make for God? whose true image, if wee iudge according to truth, is man: and there hee bringeth in the heathen saying of us; Why, haue they no altars, no temples, no knowne images? So Eusebius, Histor. Eccles. libro 7. capite 17. It was out of an heathenish custome, that the ancients did after this fort, honour those that they held to be their sauiours, (that is, with painted images.) Wee haue decreed, saith the Eliber. Councill, chap. 36. that there should bee no pictures in the Church, lest that which we worship and reuerence, should bee painted upon the walls. Epiphanius Epist. ad Ioan. Hierosolym. tore a hanging in peeces in the Church, because there was the image of a man painted thereupon, against testimonie of Scriptures. This minde of his Hierome approveth, who translated the Epistle into Latine. Hereupon some of the Papists doe reprehend Epiphanius 1. Castro contra haeres. lib. 8. titul imago, accuseth him of errour, though he cleare him of heresie: he had zeale, but not according to knowledge, saith Wolfius de sacrament. tom. 3. capite 157. Others doe reject the latter part of this Epistle as counterfeit, namely Damascene orat. de imaginib. Alan. Cope, and Sanders, but without all proofe of argument. First, they say this place is not cited in the Councill of Nicea: what then? it is cited in the Councill of Frankford, Carolus libro 4. capite 15. 2. They say Epiphanius did not reckon Image worship amongst the heresies: it is false, he directly affirmeth, Haer. 79. That it is the divels invention to make pictures of men, and set them up to bee worshipped. And againe, Haer. 55. speaking of the Melchisedechians, he saith, they made them an image of it, and worshipped it, wherein they were seduced. And amongst the heresies of the Carpocratians, Haer. 27. hee reckoneth that for one, to worship the Images of Iesus, Peter and Paul. 3. They object that of Gregory lib. 9. Indict. 4. epist. 9. unto Serenus, that broke downe the images of the Saints. Tell mee brother what [ilegible] thou hast at any time heard, or seene doe that that thou hast done. But I would have them shew that Serenus did not allowe Epiphanius and other Fathers testimonies against images.

2 About 400. yeares after Christ, images beginne to get entrance, not onely into private places, but even unto the Churches of the Christians: but the use of them was but historicall; as Augustine, De consecratione Euangel. lib. 1. capite 10. Basil, Oratione in Sanct. Barlaam. Nissenus, Oratione in [ilegible] Prudentius, Hymnus de Sancto Cassiano; and Paulinus, epistol. duodecim. doe testifie. For the bare and solitarie images of the Saints, or their single statues, were not erected untill sixe hundred yeares after Christ, which Cassander in Consult. de artic. controvers. doth plainly and freely confesse.

3 Superstition getting head, image-worship got foundation, yet neuer amongst the learned and godly; neither were images set forth for publike worship, untill sixe hundred yeares after Christ. Gregorie libro nono Indict. quart. epistol. 9. denies that images are to bee worshipped. And Sigonius, De regno Italiae, lib. primo. affirmes, that they would carrie the Virgin Maries Image in solemne pompe, but hee makes no mention of any adoration of it; even untill the yeare five hundred ninetie and one; about which time, some Councill approved the images that were then set up in Churches, but did not teach that they were to be worshipped, and if that this worship got roote any where before this time, it was not amongst the teachers, but amongst the superstitious people. Pope Sergius, saith Platina in Anno 687, in Saint Peters vestrie, found a great peece of the wood of Christs Crosse, which from that time forth, all the people upon the Exaltation day, doe kisse and adore, in the Cathedrall Church of Constantinople.

4 This same image-worshippe was first established publikely in the yeare seaven hundred eighty eight; by the 2. Nicene Councill. But on the contrary side, but a little before, a Councill of Constantinople (wherein there were three hundred and thirtie Bishops, held under Copronymus) condemned both the worship of images and Reliques. P. Aemil. de gest. Francorum. The same did Leo Constantines father, & Philippicus. Petr. Diac. lib. 6. cap. 12. And the Council of Frankford, (wherein was present Charlemaine, and the Romane legates) did condemne the second Nicene Councill as heretical. The Greekes false synode, saith Regino, lib. 2. ad an. 794. gathered for image worship, is rejected by the Pope; yea this Councill was condemned by all the Princes & Bishops of Britaine.[864] Charles the French King (saith Hoveden in continuatio Bedae ad an. 792.) sent a booke of the Synode unto Britaine, directed unto him from Constantinople: wherein (as he saith) were many things set downe quite contrary unto our true faith, but chiefly in that it was decreed by the uniforme consent of very neere all the Doctours of the Church, 300. Bishops or more in number, that images are to be worshipped: which the Church of God doth wholly detest and execrate. Against which Albinus wrote an epistle wonderously confirmed by the holy Scriptures, and in the person of our Princes and Bishops, carried it with the same booke unto the French King. Bellarmine de imag. lib. 2. c. 24. confesseth, that the Council of Frankford disallowed the Councill of Nicea; but that (saith he) happened by reason of two errours. 1. Because it thought that the Nicene Councill was called without the Popes authority. 2. Because it thought this Councill had decreed image worship to be Latria, that is, worship due to God. Now heare how hee is answered by Suarez. in 3. Thoma. quest. 25. disput. 54. I can hardly beleeve (saith hee) that the Councill of Frankford could proceede against the Nicene Councill by errour of fact; for it was gathered a little before under the same Pope Adrian that confirmed it, whose legates were present at the Councill of Frankford (as the same authors doe confesse) how then can it be that all the Fathers of this whole Councill should bee ignorant of the doctrine and authority of this Nicene Councill, having the Popes owne Legate to inlighten them in both? Now Cajetan in dialogo, [ilegible] 3. concil. and also Suarez loco praedicto, doe answer, that the Councill of Frankford defends the honour of images; and that it reproveth the Councill of Constantinople, sometime by the Greekes called the seventh, which was assembled for abolishing of Images. So the Synod of Senona, cap. 14. saith, that Charles in the Synode of Frankford did overthrow the erronious madnesse of the Iconomachi: I answer. The Councill of Frankford keepeth a mid-way reserving some honour for Images, (and so must Aemilius de gestis Francorum, libro 2. where the end; be understood, when hee saith, that Images have their reverence reserved:) and therefore condemned the Councill of Constantinople, that utterly abolished them, and the Councill of Nicea, that on the contrarie did establish the adoration of them. In the Councill of Frankford, saith Platina in Adriano, both the Synode which the Greekes call the seaventh (that is, that of Nicea) and also the heresie of Felix, concerning abolishing of Images, was taken away.

5 The Fathers generally doe not defend, but rather refute this worshippe even after the Nicene Councill. Augustine de haeres. cap. 24. doth plainly reprove the worshippers of pictures, and sepulchers. Nay this propriety, saith Hieronymus in Daniel. They say their Gods are worshipped, and images adored, both which the servants of God doe abhorre. Pictures, saith Walfridus Strabo de reb. eccl. capite 8. yet not therefore to be troden under foote, and abolished, because we know they are not to bee worshipped, nor adored. And the 6. Councill of Constantinople forbadde the picturing of the holy Ghost, under the forme of a Dove, or of the Wisemen under a starre, or of Christ under a Lambe: wherefore Caranza annot. ad canon. 82. Leo Armenius commaunded all images to be broken downe by expresse edict, Zonar. annal. tom. 3. The Almaines and Armenians forbadde the worshippe of images in their countries: Nicet. Choniat in annal. And the moderne authors teach, that the images of God are not to be made. Abulensis In Deut. 4. quaest. 5. And Durand. In 3. distinct. 9. quaest. 2. saith, That it is a foolerie to make, or adore any image of the Trinitie: where also he denies, that the images themselves are to bee worshipped, but onely the figure in the image. And, in Rationali libro primo, capite 3. Wee worshippe no images, neither call them Gods. And Biel in can. Miss. lect. 49. saith, That images are suffered in the Church, not to bee worshipped, but for other endes. So saith Hales 3. part. quaest. 30. art. 4. and [ilegible] de traditionibus. And Bishop of Aurelia, De cultu imaginum, libro 1. saith, that image-worship is pernicious, and superstitious: adding, let not our religion consist in worshipping of humane workes, for they are better that make them, and yet we ought not to worship them, let not our religion be in our phantasies. And Gerson, In compendio Theolog. expositione primi precepti, saith, Thou shalt not bow downe to them, nor worship them: betweene which distinguish thus, thou shalt not adore, that is, with bodily worship, by bowing knee or body to them; thou shalt not colere, that is, with the affect of thy minde. And a little before: wherefore images are forbidden to be made either to be bowed unto, or worshipped.

6 The Latine translatour of the Bible never observed the distinction of Imago & Idolum, as wee may see in very many places of Scripture, vid. Deut. 4. 16. and 1. King. 11. 18. Wisd. 13. and 14. Esa. 40. 18. and 44. 13. Ezech. 7. 20. imagines simulacr. Amos. 5. 23. imago idolorum. By which saith Hierome, In Esa. 37. speaking of idols, wee meane the images of the dead. So doth Cardinall Paleotus testifie, that image, picture, & idol are taken in one sense. Desiderius & [ilegible] lib. 1. capite 13. Saint Hierome (saith hee) writeth that where Idol was put in the text, Aquila translated it Imagines, or figuras. And we read in Cicero, Imagines quae vocantur Idola: Images called idols: and In Plato Idola, &c. Idols are the images, which are in the waters, or glasses, painted or printed, or such like. So the Latine word Simulachrum they alwayes put for the Greeke word Idolum: for whereas in the Latine translation of the Psalme wee reade simulacra gentium, the Images of the Gentiles, the Greek saith [griego]. And hee addeth: The name of an Image, if wee marke, the propriety of the word, signifieth any impious and divelish figure.

7 The Primitive Church bore a certaine honour and reverence unto the Reliques of the dead Saints, keeping and carrying them from place to place, and flocking unto them Hieron. contra Vigil. This honour began about 300. yeares after Christ, but they neither adored them nor bowed knee unto them for 600. yeares. For the Fathers used to put them under the altar, Ambrose lib. 10. epist. 85. sub finem; but the Papists now put them in glasses and gaudeties, above the altar, and that to have them adored. In elder times the reliques were buried in the earth, and in secret places. So Cyril contra Julian. libro 10. Cyril the Hermite, In vita Euthymij, hee removed the body of this holy man unto a Church hee had newly built, and laid it into a holy coffin, that should never after bee opened; and so saith Prudentius Peristephanon hymn. 3. of Eulalia.

The sacred bones and dust of her that sleepes, Our mother earth in hallowed bosom keepes.

And a little after.

I leave to reverence these bones so bleft: And that same clime under which they rest.

And the multitude there present, saith Victor. De persecut. Vandal. lib. 3. being full of joy, caried the bodies of the holy Martyrs unto carefull burial. So Constantine made him a bridle, and armed his helmet with the nailes that Christ was fastned to the crosse withall. Ruffin. hist. lib. 1. cap. 8.

8 At the places of these reliques (whilest the gift lasted) were sometimes miracles done, not by them, but by God to increase in us an honour to the godlinesse of their owners, not that wee should adore them, for in antiquitie, adoration was taken for humbling and prostrating the bodie.

[864] Ado also in Chron. ad an. 791. & Genebr.

### The signe of the Crosse.

1 The Fathers used to arme themselves against the devill with the signe of the Crosse, not that they ascribed any such power unto the outward figure, but because they would make shew unto others of their beliefe in the crosse, that is, in the death of Christ, with this solemne ceremonie, and use it as an item or watchword to shew forth their faith, which overcometh all evills. And the signe whereby Constantine was victor, was not the signe of the crosse, but the character of the name of Christ, which wee see in many ancient coines of Constantinus and other Christian Emperours, in forme as is in the margent here expressed: togeither with this inscription [griego] or as Socrates, lib. 1. cap. 1. Nicephorus lib. 7. capite 29. and Zonaras in Constantino, have it [griego], that is, In isto Deo, non signo, in this God, not this character. It is not requisite, saith Chrysostome, Hom. 55. in Matth. to make a bare crosse with thy finger in thy forehead, but with a strong faith in thy heart: So that the Crosse doth not signifie the figure of the crosse, but the passion of Christ crucified by a Metonymie. So saith Origen in Rom. lib. 5. And the praises given unto the signe of the crosse, are but rhetoricall tearmes, as when they call it an altar, it is a figurative speech borrowed from the ceremoniall law, and when they call is a ladder, it is a transcendent metaphor. And unto all the layings of the Fathers where they call the crosse their redemption, hope, and salvation, I answer in a word, the speeches are relatives, all referred to Christs passion, or unto himselfe in that figure represented. For it is ordinary amongst them to put the continent for the thing contained.

2 The Crosse was never adored by the ancients, much lesse adored with Divine honour: they allowed it a certaine veneration, namely a reverent use, using it in testimonie of their faith, and with all extolling it as the signe of their immoveable beliefe upon Christ crucified, before the Gentiles, yea even when they were threatned with torments. This end and use is not now amongst us, because we are not now amongst the Gentiles. Wee neither worship crosses, (saith Arnobius Contra Gentes. l. 8.) nor yet desire them; Helene (saith Ambrose, De obitu Theodos.) finding the title, adored the king (Christ he meaneth) but not the wood: because that is an error of the heathen, & an ungodly vanity. But about the 400. yeare after Christ, the Crosse began by little and little to be adored of some private men.[865] So saith Prudentius h. Apotheosis

But now the scarlet red Of th' Emperour in Christ his courts is spread: And by this mightie Prince the crosse is worshipped.

So saith Paulinus epist. 11. He (the Bishop of Hierusalem) every yeare at Easter set forth the crosse for the people to worship, being himselfe the chiefe of the worshippers. So Hierome in his epitaph of Paula, saith, that she did prostrate her selfe in adoration before the crosse, as if shee saw the Lord there hanging. And epist. 17. ad Marcellam he saith, Paula and Eustochium do wish that they might but have leave, to licke the wood of the crosse. So the Apamienses anno. 540. bringing forth the crosse, doe adore, and embrace it, Evagr. hist. eccles. lib. 4. cap. 25. But afterwards the 2. Councill of Nicea, Atlio 7. denied that Christs Image was to be adored with divine worship.

3 The Transient or passing crosse, (that is, the crosse which they signed, or the signe of the crosse) was commonly used in the purer Churches, not the fixed crosse, that is, the crosse made of stone, wood, or metall, or yet, painted upon walles in churches or oratories for the first 400. yeares. The first altar, and the first crosse were set up in England by Oswald in the field where hee conquered Cadwall, Ann. 635. Polychronic. lib. 5. cap. 12. Also in the consecration of the Sacraments the crosse was never called to use untill about the 400. yeare: for the first 300. yeares after Christ it was but held a signe of a mans outward profession, used in his ordinarie actions; but afterwards it was brought into the Lords supper; at first to signifie unto us the good wee reape by Christ, August. in Ioan. tract. 118. but afterward that by it the sacrament might bee blessed and consecrated. But that Christ did consecrate the Eucharist on this manner, Analarius utterly denyeth, De ecclesiast. offic. lib. 3. cap. 24. ascribing it unto Augustine. Besides the signe of the crosse for many ages at first, was but a simple and bare ceremonie in the sacrament, but afterward that rite being changed Ann. 1000. it since hath bin alwaies used in an odde number. Microlog. cap. 14.

4 The ancient writers held the soule to be defended by the signe of the crosse either following Montanus, as Tertullian De resurrect. carn. The bodie is signed, that the soule may be defended: or else doubtfully: I doe thinke (saith Augustine De peccat. merit. et remiss. libro 2. cap. 26. that the Catechumenists are sanctified by the signe of Christ, and prayer, with imposition of hands, after some certaine manner. Where note the words, I thinke, and, after some certaine manner, for these shew that Augustine doubted of that ceremonie, and besides you see hee held not the sanctification to bee made by the crosse onely, but with prayer also.

5 At the signe of the crosse there have miracles bin done, because the name of Christ crucified was alwayes adjoyned, either in secret or expresse invocation, and then the Saints had a power to worke miracles. Our faith (saith Tertullian, in Scorpiaco, contra Gnosticos.) is our defence, and if it be not striken with distrust when wee signe on this fashion, that is, by making this signe, we often doe good unto the heathen, God giving us that power which the Apostle shewed when hee scorned the biting of the viper. And therefore wee use this signe in miracles, and casting out of devils, are not to bee ascribed unto the crosse, but unto the faith of miracles, and invocation of Christ. How much this signe doth terrifie the devils, (saith Lactantius, De vera religione, libro quarto, capite 27.) hee may soone know, that seeth how when they are adjured by Christ, they were forced to flie from the bodies they had possessed. And a little after: Christs followers can cast out the same filthie spirits out of men, both by their masters name, and by the signe of his passion. This doth it together with the such-like calling upon Christs name, namely, the famous memorie of the victorious crosse. Stand stoutly upon this signe (saith Cyril, Catechesi 13.) for when the devils see the Crosse, they remember the crucified. To speake in a word, the Fathers give not these wonderfull effects so much unto the signe of the crosse, as unto prayer and invocation of God. Looke in the writings of all those that are of antiquitie, and see whether this be true. Looke in Nazianzene, unto Oecumenius, Origen against Celsus, libro tertio & octavo, Theodoret in his Peter and Thalassius: Eusebius in bibliot. Ecclesiastic. libro octavo capite septimo; Sulpitius unto Eusebius the priest, Epistol. prim. the Author of the Dialogues, in Gregorie Dialog. libro primo, capite primo. Victor of the persecution, by the Vandals, libro secundo; and Paulinus of the life of Saint Martin, libro secundo: all these will testifie my assertion. Nay the signe of the crosse, as the Fathers used it, was a certaine secret invocation of Christ crucified, so that it is a foolish and an idle forgerie, to say that it had that efficacie ex opera operata, by the bare making of it, seeing it had all the power from invocation.

6 Those crosses that were used in the Church for the first 400. yeares, had no image at all of Christ crucified upon them. This assertion cannot bee confuted by any approved testimonie of Antiquitie. And it seemeth that this image of the crucifixe did first grow in use publikely in or about the yeare of Grace 710. as it appeareth in the Councill held in Trullo. To the end that that which is perfected (saith this Synod, Canon. 82.) may bee represented unto publike view even in lively colours, wee command, that in stead of the old Lambe, the figure of that Lambe that taketh away the sinnes of the world, Christ our God in the likenesse of a man be set up and erected in Images, from this time forward.

[865] Distinctio adorationis & venerationis. August. [ilegible] & de doctrina christ. lib. 3. c. 9. & Caroli M. lib. [ilegible] contr. Concil. Nic. 2.

### Churches for prayer.

1 The Fathers acknowledge Churches as houses of prayer, but binde us not to come to the Church alwaies when we pray.

2 And they name their churches after their Martyrs names, for distinction sake, only appointing the worship unto God, and not unto them. Wee honour them (saith Augustine, de vera religione, capite 55.) out of charitie, not out of dutie or bond: neither build we any churches unto them. And Contra Maximinum Arrian. libro primo, titulo undecimo: Should wee not be cursed and cast out from Christs truth and his Church, if wee should build any temple of timber and stones unto any Angell, although most excellent, because wee should give that honour to a creature, which is due onely unto the Creator? If therefore wee should commit sacrilege in building a Temple unto any creature, how is not he the true God, unto whom wee build no temple, but are our selves the temple unto him? And here, as also often elsewhere, Augustine proveth the holy Ghost to bee God, because hee hath a temple. Which argument both Basill, Epistola 141. and Ambrose De Spiritu Sancto, libro tertio, capite 13. doe use.

3 The ancient consecration of the churches was with meere words and prayers, not with crossing, or such like rites. And dedication of churches began about the 300. yeare after Christ.

4 The Fathers of the first 300. yeares, never talke of adorning churches, but about Constantines time this errour got roote, and so custome bearing sway, the Fathers began to looke for ornaments for the church. Then first of all, saith Otho Frising. libro quarto, capite tertio, (in Constantines time) were publike Edicts given out for building of churches, that is, more stately roomes, or temples; for before they used holy houses to pray in.

### Canonicall houres.

THE Fathers observed houres both diversly and freely: but that all should be bound unto the same & to so many houres, is a tyrannicall superstition. And Walfridus oftentimes repeateth, that it was a long time after the Apostles that these houres were instituted and ordained. Wee must know (saith he, De reb. eccles. cap. 25.) that there passed many ages after the revelation of the Gospell, Before these houres were ordained to bee the solemnities of certaine houres in the day and night as they are now. And the purer primitive Church had not seven canonical houres: Neither Athanasius, Basill, nor Hierome doe at any time mention the first houre: Cassianus indeed doth, saying it was ordained about his time. De insti. Coenob. lib. 3. capite 4. and so doth Soto hold also, de jure & justit. lib. 10. quaest. 5. articul. 1. Wherefore Baronius saith falsely, when he affirmeth that Chrysostome and Basill doe often mention the foure houres of the day. Besides, the Fathers doe prescribe houres for the night aswell as for the day: And besides the canonicall houres, they set downe a night-service, and night-watches, as divers authors, viz. Amalarius, ecclesiast. offic. lib. 4. c. 2. ad cap. 11. Rupertus, De divin. offic. lib. 1. cap. 1. ad cap. 3. Radulphus, In Observ. can. prop. 14: Cassianus, lib. 2. cap. 4. the Councill of Agatha as it is cited Distin. 91. cap. Presbyter. Gregory in the decretals lib. tertio, tit. 41. cap. 1. de celebratione missarum. and Bede also lib. tertio in Esdram, capite 28. doth testifie. You must rise twice or thrice a night, saith Hierome to Eustochium. But they will have the middest of the night especially observed, and namely, Athanasius De virginit. Basil quaest. fusius explic. quaest 37. Hierome, Ad Eustoch. de obit. Paula, and Hugo de Sancto Victor. in speculo eccles. cap. tertio, et de eccles. offic. lib. 2. cap. primo & 9. These the Church of Rome doth not now follow, for three dayes before Easter the Priests doe sing the night service and laudes at evensong: and all the three nocturnes are sung together by the whole quire.

### Intercession, invocation, and worship of Saints.

1 Vntill 200. yeares after Christ, the intercession of the dead, and thereupon their invocation, was never heard of in the Church of God. Let any man give an instance to the contrary.

2 Afterward, Origen for one, and others, with him, fell to dispute of the intercession of the Saints for us: but very doubtfull and inconstant was their doctrine hereof, untill foure hundred yeares were expired. Whether the Saints (saith Origen lib. 2. in Epist. ad Rom.) that are with God do any thing for us, and labour,——Yet this also bee reckoned amongst the secret and hidden mysteries of God, which may not bee committed to writing. And againe, Homily 3. in Cantic. speaking of these prayers, bee saith, though not peremptorily. As for those holy men which are departed out of this world, retaining as yet their love to those remaining here behind, it shall not be amisse to thinke of them, that they have a care of their welfare, and that they helpe them with their prayers. If thou have any care (or understanding, [griego]) of our labours, (saith Nazianzene unto Gorgonius soule, in Oratio, de laudibus Gorgonia, if it bee granted unto the divine soules to know and perceive things done here below, then receive thou my prayer: And in his first oration against Julian, he saith, Heare also O thou soule of Great Constantine, if thou have any sense, perceivance, or understanding [griego]. And in his oration upon Basill, he likewise saith, that Basils soule is in heaven and there offereth sacrifice, as I suppose: [griego]. And in his Epitaph upon his father, he saith, He doth now more good with his intercession, then he did in all his life with his doctrine, as I doe perswade my selfe. And by and by he addeth: If it be not too bold a part to speake thus. So Hierome in Nepotiano his Epitaph. Whatsoever I say (quoth he) seemeth mute, because he heareth not: and yet a little after he saith, that he is amongst the quires of Angels. So Augustine in his booke of the care for the dead, cap. 16. leaves it undetermined whether the dead martyrs doe helpe us or no, and addeth, that these things passe our understanding. And cap. 13. he proveth by Scripture, and namely out of Esay the 63. 16. that the Saints know not what is done here below. And in his comment upon the 108. Psalme, hee dares not grant that the dead doe know the joyes and pleasures which happen unto their friends. The soules of the dead, saith the author of the booke de Spiritu & Anima, which is among Augustines workes, capite 19. are in a place where they neither heare nor see the things which doe here happen unto men in this life. Yet they have a care of those that live on earth, though they know not at all what they doe: even as we have a care over the dead, though not knowing what they doe. Although the Saints doe pray for us (as the Apostles did for her, meaning the woman of Canaan) yet shall wee be sooner heard when we pray for our selves, saith Theophilus, In Matthew, cap. 15.

3 Besides, the ancient writers doe commonly affirme that the soules of the faithfull are reserved in secret habitacles, (out of heaven) not enjoying the sight of God, untill the last judgement. So holdeth Irenaeus libro quinto, infine, Iustine Martyr quaest. 60. & quaest. 76. Origen homil. septim. in Levit. & lib. 2. periarch. Chrysostome homil. 39. in 1 Cor. and 18. in Hebr. Theodoret in Hebr. 11. Theophylact, In Hebr. 11. Euthymius, In Luc. capite 16. and 23. Aretas, In Apocal. capite 6. Victor, In Apocal. ibidem. Lactantius libro 7. capite 21. Hilary, In Psal. 138. Prudentius, Hymne de exequiis defunctorum. Ambrose de Cain libro secundo, cap. 2. & de bono mortis. Augustine, Retract. libro primo, capite 14. epist. 3. ad Fortunatum. Enchirid. capite 108. de Genesi ad literam, libro 12. capite 25. de civit. Dei libro duodecimo, cap. nono. & in Psal. 36. And Bernard also, Serm. de omnibus Sanctis. versic. & Serm. quart. Here it must needs follow that the Fathers either doubted of the intercession of Saints, or else contradicted themselves.

And in the same manner it may bee concluded that so they held Limbus Patrum, Invocation of Saints, and the glasse of the Trinitie.

4 Intercession of Saints, whereof the Fathers for many ages doe commonly speake, is a generall intercession for the Church, not for this or that particular man: and this intercession our Church doth very willingly acknowledge. As for that particular intercession of particular Saints, for particular men, it was not so soone beleeved, but was first of all drawne out of dreames, and rifled out of revelations. Eusebius in his historie, libro sexto, cap. 4. telleth, that Potamiena (as it was reported) three dayes after her martyrdome, appeared to Basilides in the night, setting a crowne upon his head, and telling him that shee praied unto the Lord for him. And one Apollo in a revelation saw one of his dead brethren making intercession for him: this is recorded by Palladius, in Histor. Patrum cap. 52.

5 The Fathers teach that the Saints doe make intercession for us not onely openly, by prayer, but also mystically, namely by meriting. The merits of the mother, saith Anselme libro De excellentia Maria, doe make intercession to obtaine her audience. That which we cannot bring to passe by our owne power, saith Ivo, epist. 119. wee heare may bee obtained by the merits of the blessed and perpetuall Virgin. Beleeve (saith Bern. Augustinus, Serm. secundo de S. Marco) that whatsoever you pray for by Saint Markes merits, you shall obtaine it. So the author of the epistle unto Paula and Eustochium in Hieromes workes of the assumption of Mary, saith thus of Mary: Let her commend us, with her merits, and ayd, and assist us with her prayers, that wee also may bee found worthy in her commendations. The Saints (saith the Master of the sentences, libro quarto, distinctio 45. liter. G.) doe make intercession for us, both in their merits and in their affections. Yea the Fathers sometimes give but too much unto the Intercession of the Saints. So saith Severus Sulpitius of Saint Martin, epistola secunda, that that was his onely and his last hope, that what he could not possibly obtaine by himselfe, he should merit and deserve it by Martins intercession. Wee trust and beleeve (saith Leo, Serm. 1. in natali Petr. & Paul) ——that to obtaine Gods mercy, wee must have continuall aide and assistance by the prayers of our especiall patrons, that how much ones owne sinnes doe weigh us downe, so much the Apostles merits may lift and raise us up againe. I trust (saith Prosper, lib. De promiss. & praedictiones Dei) to bee purely cleansed from all my sinnes by the prayers of the Saints. So Gregory of Tervin. Lib. quart. vita Sancti Martini in Prolog. saith, that the Saints by their intercession doe procure the everlasting punishments to bee extinguished, and the languor of our offences to be cured. And in the Fathers we shall finde the Saints our immediate intercessours with God. For so Adrian the first, Epist. ad Constant. et Irenaeus faith that the Images of the Saints are to bee worshipped, because it is certaine, that they are the servants of God, and doe continually offer up their prayers and intercession unto the Deitie for us, that doe honour them here below.

6 There can bee no Invocation of the dead proved to have beene in the Church from Christ unto 350. yeare after. For in all the Workes of the Fathers, that wrote within this time, no man is able to shew any one fit and plaine commandement or precept, nor any sincere example for invocation of Saints.

7 This invocation began first to bee brought into use in the Catholike Church, about the yeare of Grace 380. arising out of a custome of the vulgar sort, and some mens private devotions. For the Fathers of these times doe tell, how the Saints were invocated, but doe not teach that they are to be invocated. Nay in their more serious disputations and Sermons they doe reprehend the invocation of the Saints. All your vowes, all prayers, all interpellations, and all your thanksgivings (saith Origen against Celsus, libro quinto) are to be dedicated unto God the Father, the Lord of all things, by and through that high Priest, Iesus Christ, the living Word, and God. And againe: This will restraine all men from offering or daring to offer any prayers unto any person, but onely unto the Lord God, who onely is all-sufficient unto all, through the Saviour the Sonne of God. So Athanasius against the Arians, Sermone tertio, proveth Christ Iesus to bee God, because he is called upon, for a creature ought not to be worshipped. And so Epiphanius, Haeres. 79. giveth a venerable respect unto Mary, but denieth her both adoration and invocation. And Ambrose in Commentar. in Roman. prim. plainely affirmeth, that hee thinketh them fooles, that doe adore and worship their fellow-servants. And Basil, in Psalm. septimo, saith, As it is meete and fit we should worship nothing but God, so ought we not to fasten our hopes upon any but upon God. As for Hierome, hee doth not so much as in one place helpe to build up this invocation of Saints, but rather the contrarie. For writing against Vigilantius, in Epistola ad Riparium, he plainly averreth: Wee doe not worship nor adore, I doe not say, the Reliques of the Martyrs, but neither the Sunne nor the Moone, no nor the Angels,——left we should be thought to serve the creature rather then the Creator. Wee neither affirme (saith Cyril, Contra Iulian. libro 6.) that the Martyrs are Gods, neither have we accustomed our selves to adore them. And Thesaur. libro secundo, capite primo. There is no man that knoweth not that the Scriptures denie adoration unto every created nature, and allow that to God onely. Chrysostome in his true writings, doth neither use nor defend this invocation, but rather disalloweth it. As for example, in his Homily, De profectu Euangelii: But thou needest nor any patron before God (saith hee) nor with long discourse to curry favour with others, but though thou dost come alone, without ever a pardon, and offer thy prayers unto God by thy selfe, yet shalt thou obtaine thy petition: for God doth nor consent unto our request so easily, when others pray for us, as when we pray for our selves, though we be full fraught with manifold evills. Let not our religion (saith Augustine, De vera religione, capite 55.) be to worship the dead: wee are not to honour them for imitation sake, but not to worship them for religion sake. And De civit.
