Dei libro 22. capite 10. he saith: We doe not build temples unto Martyrs as unto Gods: but wee erect memorials for men departed, whose soules doe live in rest with God. Nor doe wee set up any altars to sacrifice unto them, but wee offer our sacrifice unto one onely God, both theirs and ours. At which sacrifice they are named in their order, as the Martyrs of God, who have conquered the world by confessing of him, but they are not in any wise invocated of the Priest that sacrificeth. De civit. Dei lib. 8. cap. 27. Those that defend the law, saith Theodoret in cap. 2. ad Coloss., drew on the people unto the worship of Angels also, saying that the law was given by them. And this vice remained very long in Phrygia & Pisidia. Wherefore the Synod which met at Laodicea, the Metropolitan citie of Phrygia, did by a decree prohibit all men from praying unto Angels: And unto this day there are oratories of Saint Michael to be seene amongst them and in their borders. And hereunto they did advise men out of their (exceeding) humilitie, alleadging that the God of all things is both invisible and incomprehensible, and that none can come unto him, and therefore that they must use the helpe of the Angels to obtaine the favour of God by them. So Augustine Confessionum lib. 10. cap. 42. speaking unto God, saith: Whom shall I finde that can reconcile me unto my God? shall I make meanes unto the Angels? by what prayer, or what sacraments? Looke also in the same Father in his booke De moribus eccles. capite 34.

8 The invocation which was used in these times was properly a Dialogue or conference, as with those that were present; now they were present, either by a rhetoricall fiction (as who should say, I will conceive such an one to be present) or in opinion and conceit, for then it was commonly held that the Martyrs soules were alwaies present at the places of their Martyrdome, and some beleeved them to bee everywhere. I prove both these conditions thus: Basil, and Nazianzene (as also other Fathers (having occasion given them in their Panegyricall orations) did in their conclusions not invocate their friends departed, but) as orators use to doe, speake unto them by a figure called Prosopopoeia (a faining of a person where none is) as though they were present; and make some wishes, but no prayers unto them: as when wee Englishmen playing at bowles, doe in our play bid one bowle runne, or rubbe, &c. So speaketh Nazianzen unto the Passeover. O great and holy Passeover, expiation or cleanser of the whole world, for I talke with thee as with a living creature, &c. And in Iulianum, Heare O thou soule of Great Constantine, or rather Constantius, for Constantius died when Julian was about three yeares old. Iacobi Bill. annot. 2. in hanc Orat. if thou have any sense: and a little after; What is this, O thou most divine Emperour? For I am forced to expostulate with him, as if hee were here present, and heard me, though indeed he be with God. And in his second Invective hee calleth unto Julian being dead and damned in hell. And after this manner Dionysius Areopagita Hierarch. eccles. cap. 3. part. 3. or the author of that worke under his name, hath a rhetoricall exclamation unto Christ being represented in the bread. And Victor in his booke of the Vandall persecution, speaketh unto the Patriarches, Prophets, and Apostles: And Hierom in his epitaph of Paula saith: Farewell O Paula, and by thy prayers helpe the decrepite age of him that doth honour thee: in which words there is no invocation, but an apostrophe whereby he speaketh unto her being dead, as though shee were present with him. And the same Father in Hilarius life, saith thus of Constantia: Shee was wont to watch whole nights in his sepulcher, and spake to him as if hee were present, to further her prayers. And Nyssenus likewise, Orat. in S. Theodorum. Those that behold,—saith he, doe but embrace,——as though the body were living and flourishing, using the eyes, eares, mouth, and instruments of all the senses: And there powring out the teares of love and duty unto the Martyr, as though he were living and present, they offer up their humble prayers unto him, to bee an intercessour for them, interceding him as a souldiour of God, and calling upon him, as one that obtaineth when he pleaseth. So Chrysostome, Orat. in Babylon. If any man, saith he, doe but stand by these sepulchers,——the very sight of the coffin invading his soule, doth penetrate it, and stirreth it up, moving therein such an affect, that hee seemeth them that lie there in buried, to be visibly present with him, and offering their prayers together with him. Now that it was commonly beleeved that the Martyrs soules were still present at their sepulchers, or where they would, Hieromes reprehension of Vigilantius (who denied this) doth plainly testifie. Thus, faith Hierome, contra Vigilantium, doth affirme that the soules of the Apostles and Martyrs are placed either in Abrahams bosome, or the place of re-pose, or under Gods altar, and that they cannot bee present at their tombes, and where themselves please: and he answereth him thus: If the Lambe bee every where, then those that are with the Lambe must be beleeved to be every where. And seeing the devils and evill spirits do wander all over the world, and through their too great celeritie are every where present, is it like that the Martyrs after the shedding of their blood should bee shut up in their coffins, and not be able to get out thereof? So Maximus Taurinensis, In natali Martyr. Taurinorum, saith: All the Saints are every where, and assist all men,——and are alwaies with us, and stay still with us: that is, doe both keepe and defend us while we are in our bodies, and also doe receive and entertaine us when we leave our bodies. And the like saying hath Severus Sulpitius of S. Martin epist. 2. Hee is present (saith he) with all that talke of him, and standeth by them all. But that this is very boldly affirmed, and weakly concluded, who seeth not? Though for excuse sake wee may say that these Writers used ubiq. for Passim, or ubilibet.

9 The Fathers in their prayers and communion accustomed to recite the names of the Martyrs and other Saints, desiring God withall to grant them this or that by their intreaties or intercessions. When we offer this sacrifice (saith Cyril, Catechis. 5.) wee make mention of them that are departed before us, that God may receive our prayers by their intercession. Therefore at the Communion, saith Augustine in Ioan. tract. 84. wee mention not them as we doe the others that rest in peace, or that wee should pray for them, but rather that they may pray for us. And such are the commemorations of the Saints in the liturgies that are named after Iames, Basill, Chrysostome, or that of the Church of Rome. But these publike prayers, (as also many other private ones) were but certaine vowes and desires, that the prayers which they beleeved the Saints did offer up for the whole Church, might bee beneficiall unto them before God, as George Cassander did verie well observe. Such also is the vowe of Prudentius in lib. [ilegible] in fine hymni, [ilegible] concerning the punishment of Romanus the Martyr.

Would I might chance among the Goates to stand, And be discern'd by all on the right hand; And that at his intreate the King should say, Romanus kneeles, bring me that Kidde away: Be he a lambe, and cloathed with my wooll, &c.

10 The Fathers, especially those after the 400. yeares, have agreed in the Invocation of Saints, yea are guilty even of sacrilege, for they doe sometimes put their faith, hope, and trust in them. So erred Paulinus speaking unto Felix In natali 3.

Obtaine, that God would pardon us our sinne By thy full prayers, and merits, ——

And againe, In natali 6. Lifting his soule to heaven, and comforted With faith, he hopes he hath already sped, And to Saint Felix courts with hast is carried.

And a little after, The God hath made for wearied soules a rest: Ease for the griev'd, and salve for hearts oppresst.

And in another place In natali 8. Let us unto this patrone hast, Together with hope united fast. — Wee pray thee Felix be Our right hand still, and tower of safety.

And so saith Fortunatus of Martin, in his life, lib. 2. Reverend, whom I with heart and voyce adore, Helpe me poore wretch, it's mercy I implore.

And presently after: O blessed Mediator be Betweene my grieved Lord and me.

And so Leo, Serm. 1. de nat. Petr. & Paul. c. 7. saith, that look how much our own sinnes do cast us downe, so much the Apostles merits doe raise us up. And Gregor. hom. 32. in Evang. Make these the protectours of you in your guilt, saith he, libro 22. epistol. 21. Wee hope in the vertue of Almighty God, and of Peter the prince of the Apostles. So Ephrem, Fulgentius, and Damianus doe all exceede all meane in the prayses of the blessed Virgin. Hee hath magnified thee, (saith Damianus, de nativ. Mariae. Sermo. 2.) that is mightie, and unto thee is given all power in heaven and earth, and nothing is impossible unto thee to whom it is possible to elevate those that are desperate, unto hope of blessednesse. For how can that power hinder thy power, which tooke flesh of thy flesh? For thou commest unto that Golden altar of mans reconciliatio, not onely as king, but even commanding; not as a servant, but as a Lady, and mistresse. And sometime they sticke not to say, that they doe know all things: as Paulinus, natal. 6.

Thou knowest their mansions that in Christ is light. Seest all, though hidde and absent from thy sight. And in th' acknowing God, knowst every thing aright.

So likewise holdeth Prosper de vita contempl. libro 1. capite 4. Nothing (faith he) shall bee hidde from the perfect, who are to see God himselfe, which is better then all these, with their pure hearts.

11. The use of invocation which in elder times had beene but private mens custome, about the 500. yeare, began to become publike: for then begunne Petrus Gnaphaus to shuffle the invocation of Saints, amongst the prayers of the Church: for it is called his invention to name the virgin Mary, and to invocate her divine name in every prayer. Niceph. libro 15. capite 8. And about the 600. yeare, Gregory the great commaunded a Litany to be publikely sung, wherein all the Saints were invocated. So that the commemoration of the Saints was at that time turned into invocation.

12 This opinion of Invocation of Saints had a large part of the originall from dreames, visions, doubtfull and uncertaine revelations, yea and was most of all confirmed by such meanes. It fell out, saith Sigebertus, De reg. Ital. libro 1. that which way soever the Image (of the Virgin Mary) was carried, the mortall pestilence of the ayre did depart, & good health followed: for which blessing all men giving thankes, an Angell was heard out of heaven, speaking unto the blessed Virgin, in these words: Rejoyce O Queene of heaven, alleluiah, because hee whom thou deservest to beare alleluiah, is risen againe, according to his word; alleluiah, which speech when Gregory heard, being forthwith inspired by the holy Ghost, hee thus concluded it: pray for us unto God, alleluiah, ad ann. 594. So one Conradus a Germane, penitent for his sinnes, comming unto Rome, Hildebrand then Pope, commaunded him to weare a coate of mayle in stead of his shirt, and fastened in with five chaines; giving him sealed letters, containing the catalogue of his sinnes, and commanding him to goe visit all the holy places of the earth, to try if hee could obtaine any pardon or remission for his sinnes. When hee had continued in prayer from the first houre of the day untill the ninth, (in Saint Steven the kings tombe in Hungarie) falling into a dead sleepe before the altar, the holy king appeared unto him. Arise my friend (quoth hee) thou shalt obtaine no pardon of God by any merits, or helpe of mine; but goe unto my son Emerikes tombe, which is here hard by, and hee by his virginity hath deserved chiefe favour with God. Hee awaking out of his dreame, invocated the name of that Saint, & swifter then thought, his chaines wherewith hee was bound, burst all in peeces, his letters opened of themselves (the seale being broken up) wherin there was no one sinne, no nor one letter to be read or seene. And from that time forward, the chappell was had in such reverence, that men came unto it from the furthest countries. Bonfinius lib. 3. decad. 2.

13. The power of Canonizing was never heard of with the fathers, untill the yeare 880 and then Adrian took up this authority. And Alexander the third after him confirmed it in his decrees, cap. 1. Extra. de reliquijs Sanctorum.

14 The distinction of religious worship into Dulia (saint-worship) and Latria, (God-worship) the Apostles never knew, nor the Greeke Fathers, nor the Latines for at least 400. yeares after Christ. For the Scripture in divers places ascribeth Latria (in the greek translation) unto men: Deut. 28. 48. Levit. 19. 8. and in other places Dulia is attributed unto God, Rom. 16. 18. So Augustine granteth Latria unto men, de civit. Dei, lib. 10. cap. 1. and denieth them religious Dulia. de vera relig. c. 55. Wee honour the Saints (saith he) with charity, not with service, that is Dulia. And here observe first, that Augustine denies Dulia unto Saints. And quest. 94. in Exod. he giveth both Latria & Dulia unto God, Latria as to God, Dulia as to the Lord. Secondly, by Latria and Dulia he distinguisheth religious worship from civill worship. de civit. Dei, lib. 10. c. 1. & 4. Thirdly, Latria is alwaies used in the Scriptures for service, as he affirmeth, much lesse that it should bee any thing more then Dulia, de civit. Dei. l. 5 c. 15. & l. 6 c. 1. & l. 7 c. 32. & l. 10 c. 1. & 4. Indeed Dulia politicus, that is, service used in a civill stare, was alwaies received, and so ought to be still by al men, Gal. 5. 13. But that Dulia which is higher then civill worship, was not given to men for 400. yeares after Christ. And no wonder: for Seruitude is commonly a greater thing, and used for servitude without any wages, because he that serveth is in another power. But Suidas [griego] that the word Latria signifieth a service for hyre. Hereupon Perefius de trad. part. 1. confid. 7. disproveth the name Dulia being taken for saint worship, because he will have it given unto God, not unto men, as they are Gods servants: unlesse you take the name of service metaphorically and not properly. So Laurence Valla, and Lodwicke Vives, In Aug. de civ. Dei, libro 10 capite 1. doe both take Latria and Dulia for one thing, and in one sense. Wherefore this distinction was invented by men of the later ages, which indeede Bellarmine doth acknowledge. How bee it, it is in Bede upon Luke, in cap. 4. and in Lombard, and all his followers, in Sentent. lib. 3. distinct. 9.

15 That Christs Image is to be worshipped with Latria, is denyed by many. As by Henricus Quodlibet. 1. q. 6. (who saith it must be worshipped but with hyperdulia.) Albertus Magnus, In Maria cap. 81. Francis Maira, in 3. sent. distinct. 9. Gabriel, lect. 49. in Canonem, and Perefinus in his booke de traditionibus part. 3. The second Nicene Councill, Actione 6. 3. giveth worship unto Images, but denieth them Latria: and this Latria was not given unto Christs Image for 1000. yeares after him. This doth Catharinus freely confesse in his booke de Imaginum cultu, where also hee affirmes, that Thomas never read that councill of Nice.

16 The Glasse (or Idea) of the Trinitie wherein the Saints are said to see our prayers, is a meere fiction, unknowne unto the Fathers for the space of many ages after Christ. Augustine in his booke of the care for the dead, cap. 13. affirmeth, that the soules of the departed never know what we doe here upon earth, and doth bring for proofe thereof that of Esay the 63. 16. Abraham hath not known us: and that of the Kings 2. King. 22. I will gather thee to thy Fathers, ——— that thine eye see not the destruction which I will bring upon this place. And the Fathers of the first foure ages after Christ, did commonly affirme, that the Saints were present with those that called upon them, and therefore heard them: yet was not this opinion approved of all the latter writers, for some of them doe deny, that the soules of the godly doe know our prayer in the word, or divine essence, as Durandus distinct. 39. quest. 3. Soto ibid. quest. 3. art. 3. con. 8. & Cajetane, In Thomae 3. part. quest. 10. art. 2. but onely in their proper kinde by particular revelation.

17 The worshippe given unto the Saints, whereof the Fathers commonly speak, was a worshippe, of love, societie, veneration, and honouring of them, in imitation, gratulation, esteeme, praise, and holy remembrance of them, belonging unto the second table: and not any religious worshippe or adoration: because that at first they were not worshipped with Churches, oblations, nor appointed service, as they were afterwards, and are at this day in the Church of Rome. This doth Augustine testifie in three severall places, viz. In Psal. 88. De civit. Dei. 8. cap. 27. Contra Faust. libro 20. capite 4. & 21. and Eusebius likewise affirmeth, Hist. libro 4. capite 15. And Alexander Ales. q. 92. memb. 1. art. 4. disputeth, that God alone is simply to be called upon; and the Saints are rather of the number of those that pray continually, then of him that is prayed unto: and this did Cassander very well observe in him, In consultatione (super art. con-troversiae 21.)

18 The vowes which now adaies are made unto the Saints, were altogether unknowne till Lombard his time: for he doth define a vowe, dist. 38. In. A. to be a certaine testifying of a voluntary promise, which ought properly to bee made concerning God, and the things that belong unto God.

### Prayers for the dead.

1 Before 170. years after Christ there were no memories of Martyrs kept in Churches, nor any prayers, offerings, or sacrifices for the dead, until 200. yeares after the passion. The first mention of them is in Tertullian, and they had their beginning from tradition, as he affirmeth in his booke de corona militis: Of these and other orders (saith hee) if you require the reasons, you shall finde no Scripture for them, tradition will be pretended for the increase, custome for the confirmer, and faith for the keeper hereof.

2 The Fathers of the first 400. yeares were of opinion, that we must pray for all the dead, even for the faithlesse & the damned: yet are they uncertaine whether the dead may bee helped any thing by our prayers and almes-deedes, or no: and if in any place they set downe any certainty hereof, yet not in that sense the Papists now doe hold it.

The Sacrifices (saith Augustine Enchir. c. 110) either of the Altar, or of almes-deeds, are propitiations for the dead which were not very wicked: and for the very wicked, they are meanes (saith hee doubtfully) to make their damnation the more tolerable.

And so holdeth Prudentius, lib. Cathemerinon, in hymno 5. ad incensum cerei paschae. Yearly that night, wherein our Lord arose From the Acherontike lake, the cage of woes, The torments of th' afflicted ghosts doe stay, And all the damned crue keepe holy-day.

And a little after: Then hell doth slumber in soft punishment: And all the soules in that vaste prison pent, Rejoyce in rest: the fire then burnes not sore, Nor boyle the floods with sulphure, as before.

Of these prayers Chrysostome speaketh very doubtfully, Hom. 3. in Philip. Say, I pray thee, (quoth he) what hope can remaine for them that goe from hence burdened with their sins, unto a place where they cannot bee disburdened of them? for whilest they were in this world, there was still hope and expectation that they would be converted, and become better men. —— Let us helpe them so farre as wee may; let us procure them some ease, (though it can be but little) yet let us helpe them somewhat: —— this yet affordeth some comfort unto them. And afterward he will have us to pray for all the dead, as we do for all the living, for theeves and robbers, because perhaps there may bee some conversion of them. And in this manner doubteth hee in divers places, viz. Hom. 69. ad pop. Antioch. & 70. Againe, Hom. 21. in Act. If we doe offer (saith he) continuall prayers, and give continuall almes for him, though hee be unworthy of them, yet God will bee more pacified towards us. —— And Hom. 32. in Matt. Vnto thy dead sonne give his due, that therewith he may cleanse away his spots of sinne from him. So Epiphanius Haref. 75. confesseth these prayers to have no foundation in Gods word, but onely are appointed by the Church to be made, and that they doe behoofe the dead, although they doe not take away the guilt of the whole fault. [ilegible] bringeth in certaine examples, to proue that the prayers of the faithfull doe in some part helpe the unfaithfull, and such as are damned unto everlasting torments. And yet in the same place, speaking of the opinion, whether the soules of the Christians may by almes deedes be released of their paines, and so the freeing of the ungodly out of hell, he saith thus: But we define or determine nothing, onely we reason of brotherly love. And a little after; Then is there no time to seeke helpe for every man shall beare his owne burden: but now is the time of aide, now the time of entreaty, now is the time of reconciliation.

Augustine de cura pro mort. c. 5. is uncertaine whether prayers for the dead are of any efficacie or no: and if he beleeved that his soule was helped by the Martyrs merits, this beleefe was a kinde of supplication, and helped him that way, if he had any help any way. And ch. 1. he affirmeth these prayers to be according unto the use of the Church. After the same manner he doubteth also in other places, de Civit. 21. 27. And truly it is very likely that this kinde of prayer had his first spring from the Montanists, the inventors of Purgatory. Looke Tertullian in his booke de castitate & monogamia. But there were some that disallowed of these prayers, as Gratian can testifie, c. 13. q. 2. cap. In praesenti. in one place citing Hierome in Gal. 6. saying thus: In this life we may help one another by prayers, or by good counsell: but when we come before the judgement seat of Christ, then neyther Iob, Daniel, nor Noah can speake for any man, but every man must carry his owne burthen. And Petrus Cluniacensis, l. 1. ad Petrobrusianos, confesseth plainly, that there have beene some Catholikes that have doubted of this praying for the dead. And so Augustine saith, Ser. 17. de verb. Apost. He injureth a Martyr, that prayeth for him.

3 The prayers for the dead in their first beginning were but thanksgivings and praises, wherein the Martyrs names were yearely rehearsed. So Cyprian speaking of Martyrs, Epist. 5. lib. 4. faith, We offer continuall sacrifice for them. And Epiphanius haer. 75. contra Aerium, Let us solemnize the memories of all the just, the Prophets, Patriarkes, Apostles, Euangelists, Martyrs, Confessours, and Bishops: whom a little before hee affirmed to live with God. And in like manner faith Chrysostome Homil. 12. in Act. It is offered for the Martyrs, and for all the faithfull departed.

4 The Fathers prayed for the dead, not that they might have remission of their sins, as touching the temporall paines of Purgatory (for they prayed for all the dead in generall without exception; as Cyril testifies, c. 5. Myst.) wherefore their prayers were made for other ends, and namely, to shew their zeale unto them, & their desire to commend them unto God. So doth Ambrose concerning his brother Satyrus, in these words: Thou (O Almighty God) doe I commend his innocencie, unto thee I doe offer my sacrifice: Graciously and favourably accept of a brothers gift and a priests sacrifice. Now lest we should suppose him to be in Purgatory, he had said before, He is entred into heaven, because hee beleeved on the word of God. And likewise upon the death of Valentinian, he saith, No day shall be passed by me in silence of you, no speech of mine shall passe without your honourable mention, no night shall bee spent without some prayer of mine bestowed upon you, and in all mine oblations shall I remember you often. But he had said before, Let us beleeve that he is gone up out of the desert, that is, out of this barren and evill tilled earth, unto those sweete and pleasant delights, where being adjoyned unto his brothers company, he liveth in eternall felicity. As also of Theodosius hee saith thus, Theodosius liveth in the light, and glorieth in the armies of the Saints. And yet before he had prayed for him also in these words: Graunt that consummate repose unto thy servant Theodosius, that rest which thou hast prepared for all thy Saints. And in like manner Augustine beeing about to pray for his mother Monica, Conf. libro 9. capite 13. saith, I beleeve O Lord that thou hast already fulfilled my request: but Lord approove my voluntary petitions. So Matthew of Westminster saith, that Charles about the yeare 797. wrote unto Offa king of Mercia, to commaund his subjects to make intercession for Pope Adrian: yet he addeth, having no doubt that his soule is in rest, but onely to shew our most deare love and affection unto him. 2. The Fathers prayed for the dead, to cherish the hope of the resurrection & the desire of hastening it on. So Ambrose orat. de Valent. saith, Wee pray thee Almighty God to raise up these two yong men (Valentinian and Gratian) with a timely resurrection, and recompence their untimely course of this life, with as timely a resurrection. 3. They pray for them, that their glory doe increase untill the day of judgement, and that then their sinnes bee not imputed unto them, So saith Chrysostome, hom. 32. in Matt. Dost thou thinke he departed in the corruption of sinne? Give him his own wherewith he may cleanse himselfe from the blots thereof. Dost thou thinke he departed in the purity of righteousnesse? Give him of thine, that his reward and payment may bee the more ample. And the Fathers used to offer their prayers in this manner: Graunt we beseech thee (O Lord) that this offering may benefit the soule of blessed Leo. Witnesse Innocentius the third, in his decretals, cap. Cum Marthae, extra de celeb. miss. 4. They pray for them that their damnation might be the more tolerable. So saith Aug. in his Enchiridion, c. 110. & 111. They may thinke (if this please them) that the paines of the damned soules at some certaine times are somewhat mitigated: even so, that we must still understand that the wrath of God, that is, their damnation remaineth still unto them. In this sense Paulinus, epist. 19. prayes for ease for a soule that was tormented in hell: and no marvell, since Prudentius, Cathemerin. hymno 9. de Pasch. (before him) doth affirme that at such and such tides

The torments of th' afflicted Ghosts doe stay, And all the damned crue keepe holy-day.

Damascene affirmeth, Orat. de defunct. that Trajan and Falconilla were delivered out of hell by the prayers of Gregory and Tecla. Wherefore these prayers were properly the vowes of such as wished them happinesse, or else they were thanksgivings: and in these the Fathers regarded the fulnesse or end of the time, not the middest of it: for they beleeved all the Saints to be kept in one common place of custody untill the last judgement, & therefore they wished the region of light and peace unto all good men. And albeit they thought the dead to be helped by the prayers of the living, yet they held not this benefit to fall unto them being in Purgatory, but rather then in heaven or hell. 5. Their prayer for the dead was an admonition unto the living, of the goodnesse of God unto the dead, and of the future reward which they should obtaine in following their vertues. So saith the author of the booke cal'ed Hierarchia Ecclesiastica, c. 7. And therefore the Fathers prayed for the dead for other ends, then the Papists now adaies doe.

5 Offrings for the dead at the first were not sacrifices of expiation, but only Eucharisticall, that is, thanksgivings, or banquets, and gifts and legacies of the dead unto the poore, given as almes, and as we here in England call them Doales: as also they were foundings of Churches and schooles, or yearely annuities bequeathed unto either of them.

When wee celebrate the memory of the Saints (saith Ephrem, lib. de pen. cap. 2.) if it bee the true Ephrem whole book we have. Let us remember the sicke, the widowes, the fatherlesse, the poore, and the travellers. And hereupon after the death of any one in the primitive Church, they sung alleluiah. The breath was no sooner out of her mouth (saith Hierome in his Epitaph of Fabiola) but the report of it gathered the whole city together unto her funerall; —— the Psalmes sounded and the alleluiah resounding aloft, did shake the guilded roofes of the temple.

So Epiphanius, Haref. 75. and Chrysostome, Ad popul. Antioch. hom. 70. & hom. 4. in Heb. affirme, that they used to carry lamps and tapers, and sing hymnes at the funerals of the dead, to signifie glory and praise unto God, that had vouchsafed already to crowne the soule departed with felicity. Of this nature also was their offerings at marriages, at birth dayes, &c. being all instituted for memories and gratulations, though afterward about Gregories time, when superstition got head, they were all changed into redemptions of soules out of Purgatory..

Therefore Prayer for the dead, that they might bee freed from their veniall sinnes, and from that temporall punishment for their mortall sinnes, which they are to endure in Purgatorie, was never taught nor admitted by the Fathers;

### Justification.

1 Augustine, and the rest of the Fathers that dispute against Pelagius, doe take Justice for an inherent sanctity, or new obedience: Grace for the assistance of the holy Spirit: and to justifie, for to make one from unjust, just. But indeed they hold with us, that this new obedience is not in this life perfected, and that we doe satisfie Gods judgements, and attaine unto everlasting life onely by the sole obedience of the death of Christ, Looke their expositions upon 2. Corinthians, capite quint. vers. 21. For so saith Augustine, De verbis Apostolorum, Serm. ext. ——— That wee may bee Gods righteousnesse in him: marke here two things: Gods righteousnesse, and not ours: and that in him, and not in us. And in his booke, De Spirit. & liter. cap. 26. Justification belongeth not to the doers of the law, but goes before them that fulfill it. Or els it is so said, they shall be justified, as if it were said, they shall be taken for just, or accounted just. And de fide & operibus cap. 14. Epist. 120. cap. 30. Good workes doe follow him that is justified, and not goe before him that is to be justified. And againe, expositio inchoat. epist. ad Romanos: Men being justified by beleefe, doe thenceforth beginne to live righteously. So Hierome likewise in 2. Corinthians 5. saith: So Christ was offered for our sinnes, taking upon him the name of sinne, that wee might be made the righteousnesse of God in him, nor our owne, nor in our selves. And so saith Chrysostome ibid.: He made the just a sinner, thereby to make the sinners just. Nay, he said not thus, but farre more powerfully: For he affirmeth not thoroughly, but the substance is, he saith not, a sinner, but sinne: that we might be made (he saith not) righteous, but righteousnesse, and so the righteousnesse of God: for that righteousnesse is of God, seeing we are justified not of workes (wherein it is necessary, that there be not spot or staine) but of Grace. And againe, in his 17. Homily upon the tenth of the Romanes, he saith in like manner: If thou hast beleeved in Christ, thou hast both fulfilled the Law, and farre more then it commanded: for thou hast already received a farre greater righteousnesse. And Anselme, in secund. ad Corinthios capite quint. saith plainely: God made Christ sinne for us: that wee might be made the righteousnesse of God in him. Hee therefore was made sinne as we are made righteousnesse, neither is that righteousnesse ours, but Gods; (that is, it is not of our selves, but of God;) nor in our selves, but in him: as he was made sinne, not his owne sin, but ours; neither was the sinne in himselfe, but in us. So Bernard, Serm. ad milit. Templi, cap. 11. saith: Furthermore, death is chased away by Christs death, and Christs justice is imputed unto us. And Epist. 190. Man hath another justice assigned unto him, lacking his owne—— One mans satisfaction is imputed unto all; And in his 61. Sermon upon the Canticles: Lord I will remember thy justice onely, for it is also mine: For thou art made righteousnesse unto me of God. Shall I bee affraid that one cannot suffice for us both? it is no short raiment unsufficient to couer two: thy justice is an everlasting justice, and will cover both thee and me also, and that largely, being most large, and most lasting. Nay, some of the moderne writers doe acknowledge this imputative justice: as the [ilegible] of Colen doth [ilegible], and Albertus Pighius himselfe, controv. secund. in these words: If we speake formally and properly, we are not justified by our owne faith or charity, but by the onely justice of God in Christ, that is, the onely justice of Christ being communicated unto us.

2 The Fathers howsoever they doe speake differently, and undoubtedly, of this place of justification: yet in their serious meditations, and when they were entangled with controversies, they never fled unto any justice by workes, or unto any merits. Heare what Ambrose faith, Epist. 71. Let no man glory in his workes, because no man is justified by his deeds: but he that hath justice, hath it [ilegible]: because after baptisme he is justified: it is therefore faith that freeth him through the blood of Christ, because happy is he that hath his sinnes forgiven, & his pardon granted. And Augustine crieth out, Confess. lib. 13. c. 13. Woe also be unto the man of most commendable life, if you sift his actions without the fauour of mercy. Onely Christ (saith he ad Bonif. lib. 4. c. 4) did undergoe punishment for us without any evill desert, that we might attaine unto grace by him, without any good desert. And Serm. 49. de Tempore: What is that? Enter not into judgement with thy servant: Stand not in judgement with mee, nor exact of mee all that thou hast commanded me, and injoyned me: for thou wilt find mee guilty, if thou enter but in judgement with mee: wherefore I stand in need of thy mercy, rather them of thy most easie judgement. And, De grat. & lib. arb. cap. sept. If that thy good deserts be Gods gifts, then doth not he crowne thy good deserts as thine owne deservings, but as his owne gifts. And, in Psalm. 67. The ungodly is justified by faith without anie good deserts of his workes. Besides, & de spiritu & litera, cap. 13. We doe gather out of many testimonies, that man is not justified by the precepts of good life, but by the faith of Iesus Christ. And such a speech hath Basill in his Commentaries upon the 114. Psalme: Eternall rest is prepared for those that have resisted the devill strongly in this life; not as a debt give to their workes, but out of the bounteous grace of the most mighty and mercifull God. And in his Commentary upon the 32. Psal. If by himselfe the judgment of God were sufficient, & if he should deale with us severely according unto our merits, what hope were there remaining for any of us? which of us all should be saved? Hilary in like manner, Psal. 51. affirmeth that those workes of justice are not of themselves sufficient to merit perfect blisse, unlesse that Gods mercy even in this will and desire of justice, doe not impute the viciousnesse of mans motions and changes unto him. Let a man attaine unto perfection never so much (saith Hierome in Ezech. lib. 14. cap. 46.) yet shall he stand in need of mercy for all that: and cannot attaine unto the fulnesse of perfection by his merits in this life, but onely by Grace.

It is Gods purpose (saith Primasius, in Romanos, cap. 8.) to justifie man, without any workes of the Law, or any other merits whatsoever, by faith alone: this is a wonderfull thing, saith Saint Chrysostome, Sermon. 2. Ad Ioan. in Roman. capite quarto: that he who became so famous for his worthy acts, could not bee justified by his good workes, but by his faith: herein is the power of faith mightily manifested. And so saith Paulinus, epistol. decim. ad Sever. Although wee are able to keepe his commandements (with his helpe), yet ought wee perforce to acknowledge our unprofitable service, because wee cannot impute unto our selves a just execution of our duty, if wee keepe the commandements onely. And in the same sense saith Marcus the Hermite in his booke de Lege spirituali: Whosoever wee bee that are thought worthie the washing of the new birth, wee doe not good workes for any retribution sake, but onely for the keeping of that puritie and cleannesse which is committed unto us. And a little before, The kingdome of heaven is not a reward for any workes, but the meere grace of God prepared for his faithfull servants. And Gregorie the great also, Mor. libro 9. capite 14. & libro 21. capite 15. doubts not to affirme, that all mans justice would be found to be injustice, if God should use a strict judgement. And libro 9. capite 7. This justice of ours being tried upon the touchstone of the divine justice, will be found injustice, and it is filthy in the discussion of the Iudge, though it shew faire in the estimation of the doer. And libro 9. capite 14. I grow strong unto life, not by merits, but by pardon. And capite 18. Note that the holy man saith not, my hands shined being most pure: but my hands shined as most pure; because as long as wee are bound under the punishment of corruption, though we take never so much paines in doing good workes, yet shall wee never attaine unto true puritie. And the same Father in his seaventh homily upon Ezechiel sub finem, saith, Let us repose no hope in our teares, nor in our deedes, but in the mediation of our advocate: And in his Commentaries upon the full penitentiall Psalme: I doe not intreate thee to save mee, trusting to mine owne merits, but presuming to obtaine that out of thine onely mercy, which I despaire to doe out of mine owne deservings.

Eusebius Emissenus in like manner confirmeth our assertion thus: Though wee sweate in toyle of soule and body, saith he, and exercise all our power in obedience, yet shall wee never attaine by any desert to get the kingdome of heaven, as a recompence for them. And Bernard, Sermon. 10. de Adventu. Thou canst never merit the glory eternall, unlesse it be give thee freely, —— nor are mans merits of that value to claime heaven as their just due. And Serm. in cant. 23. It is sufficient for me unto all righteousnesse, to have him my favourer, to whom only I have given cause of offence: all that he doth not impute unto me is as though it were not at all. Not to sinne is Gods justice, & mans iustice is Gods pardon.

This also Anselme upon Rom. 12. directly affirmeth. Because all men (saith he) were infolded in sinne, therefore thenceforth salvation consisteth not in mans merits, but in Gods grace. And in his Meditations: My life doth terrifie me, for if it be diligently examined, it appeareth wholly either sinne or barrennesse. And if there bee any fruit therein, it is either so fained, so imperfect, and some way so corrupted, that it cannot but either not please, or displease God. Truely it is either wholly in sinne and damnable, or barren & contemptible. But this of Anselme is most of all to be noted. In this death alone (saith he) place all thy trust; unto this death commit thy self wholly, with this death cover thy selfe wholly, and therein inwrappe thy selfe wholly:[866] If God will judge thee, say, O Lord, I put the death of our Lord Iesus Christ betwixt mee and thee and thy judgement; no other wise doe I stand out with thee: If he say, thou hast deserved damnation; say then, I put the death of my Lord Iesus Christ betwixt me, and my evill deservings, I offer the merits of his most worthy passion, for the merits which I should have had, and also have them not. And Bellarmine free confession hereof is not to bee overpassed with silence, de Iusti.lib.5 cap.7. Because of the uncertainty of our owne justice (saith he) and the danger of vaine glory, it is most safe and sure to place all our trust upon the onely mercy and benignitie of God.

3 The Fathers sometimes speake unfitly of the article of justification, and that because of three errours: 1.Because they speake of justification rather like Philosophers then Divines, bending their divinitie unto the likenesse that morall Philosophy bore then amongst the Gentiles, thereby the more easily to gaine the more of them unto God. Looke in Clements of Alexandr. Stromat. 1.2. Because they confound the Law and the Gospell, not distinguishing the justice of the one from the justice of the other, as Origen hom.6.in Levi. saith: It is Gods Law that washeth thee and purgeth thy sinnes. 3. Because they extolled mans naturall strength too much: for Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clemens, Iustine, and Epiphanius held also, that men were saved by the law of nature and by Philosophy.

4 The distinction of justification into the first and second, was not knowne amongst the Fathers for 1500. yeares after Christ, but is an invention of this age.

5 The Fathers doe often speake improperly of justification, according unto common use, putting sometimes the word of justification for sanctification, or the renewing of the whole man, both according unto nature, and manners, and this they will have done by inward vertues and workes.

6 The Fathers affirme that workes do justifie onely declaratively, not effectively. So saith Thomas upon the 2. of Iames. The workes that follow faith are said to justifie, not as justification is called an infusion of justice, but as it is called an exercise, a shewing, or a consummation. And then a thing is said to bee done, when it is perfected and made knowne.

7 The Fathers sometimes speake hyperbolically of workes, thereby to take away the carelessenesse of the vulgar, and set them on fire with a greater desire unto good workes, unto this end doe Chrysostomes words ad popul. Antioch. Homil.33. send, when he saith, that Almes doe free a man from death, (from hell, he meanes) giveth eternall life, & are advocates for us: as also that of Hilary, in Matth. Cap.6. we must of our selves deserve eternall life. And Ambrose, de poenit. l.2. c.5. faith in the same sense: Our sinnes are covered by our workes. So doth Origen, hom.1. in Exech. Why dost thou thinke much to labour, contend, and endeavour, and by thy good workes to be the cause of shine owne salvation & blisse?

__________
[866] Vlenberg. 1. de caus cur Euseb. pag. 436.

### Merit

1 Merit taken in his proper sense, for due and just desert, was never allowed of the found professors for a thousand years after Christ. So that to merit, in the Latine Fathers doth signifie to doe something which is acceptable and pleasing unto God, and worthy of account; and to obtaine, or get any thing of God, even without any desert of ours. A sincere and peaceable prayer, saith Cyprian, deserved (or merited) the Lord, (that is, obtained his favour.) And Sulpicius in the life of Martin, saith, Let him imitate Ottanius in deserving his fellowes, that is, in getting their good wills by doing them good turnes. And so saith Ambrose, libro 10. in Luc. capite 22. in the beginning. O Water, which deservedst to bee the Sacrament or mysterie of Christ, which washest all, and art not washed thy selfe &c. So Pope Cornelius, in Eusebius, lib.6. cap.4. saith of Novatus, that hee was not confirmed of the Bishop by the signe, and added, [griego] which words [griego] Rufinus.c.3. translateth thus: Vnde nec spiritum sanctum potuit promereri: wherefore hee could not deserve (that is, obtaine) the holy Ghost. So Augustine Epist. 11. writeth unto Hieromy: I have not yet deserved thy writings: and elsewhere Epist. 13. would to God I could deserve to be embraced of thee. And Serm. 49. de temp. Let no sinner despaire of himselfe, since Paul deserved pardon: and Tract. 3. in Ioan. to the like effect hee saith, that we doe deserve God by faith, that is, wee are acceptable unto him. And that of Gregory is most note worthie: O happy fault which deserved to have such a redeemer.

2 Merit in the writings of the Fathers is not put for the worthinesse of the good worke in the respect of the reward, but it is alwaies put for the good worke it selfe, pleasing unto God, and accepted of him, not of it selfe, and it owne worthinesse, but through the divine favour, and free acceptation of all good workes in Iesus Christ. And therefore it is so called, namely, a good worke, thereby to incite us the more to doe these good things. This doth Cardinall Bellarmine freely confesse, lib.2. de grat. & lib. arbit. cap.12. And that the word Merit is to be taken in this sense, it hereby appeareth, because all the Fathers doe ascribe all things unto grace wholly. As Bernard, Serm.63. in Cant. saith, my Merit is Gods mercy: and the same word Merit, in his true, and proper sense is by them opposed against grace; as the same Bernard useth it, Serm.67. in Cant. There is no place for grace to enter where merit hath taken up all before: And besides, Serm.68. It is sufficient unto merit to know that our merit is insufficient; wherefore these workes of grace are called merits by a metaphor, not properly, because they are the gifts of God: as life everlasting is called a wage: not properly, but metaphorically. And unto this end doth Bernard direct his doctrine in his first sermon of the Annunciation, saying, that merits in very deede, doe deserve nothing. Neither are mans merits of such worthinesse (quoth he) that life eternall should bee their due; or that God should any waies injure man, in not giving it unto him: for (to omit that all mans merits are wholly the gifts of God, and that man is rather a debtor unto God for them, the God any waies unto him;) what are all our merits, being compared with that so admirable glory? And the distribution of rewards is of Gods grace, not the wage of merit, because (as Fulgentius saith very well, ad Monimum lib.1. cap.10.) It is very rightly called grace, because God doth not onely accumulate his gifts upon his gifts, but also, because the bountie of the Divine retribution is shewed in such quantity, that it doth admirably and incomparably exceeding all merits, though proceeding from a will and operation both good and given of God. And even the same saying hath Radulphus Ardens, in Dominica 18. post Trin. Because (saith he) we proceed from and by one grace, unto another, wee can but improperly call them merits: for as Augustine againe beareth witnesse, God doth crowne nothing in us, but his owne grace. And againe, in eodem Dom. Septuag. to the like effect: Let no man thinke that God is as it were bound by covenant to performe his promise; for as he is free to promise, so is he free to pay, chiefly seeing our merits as well as our rewards are of his grace: For God crowneth nothing but his grace in us, who if he would deale strictly with us, no man living should be justified in his sight. And therefore the Apostle, that tooke more paines then all, saith, The sufferings of this life are not worthy of that future glory which shall be revealed: wherefore his bargaine is nothing else but a voluntary promise.

3 Also Merit sometimes signifieth the dignitie and excellencie of the thing in it selfe, as when Hierome in Epistul. Evagr. saith: All Bi-shops are of the same merit, and the [ilegible], so the Fathers say virginitie is of a greater merit then the other vertues: but indeed merit doth seldome signifie that which we in England call desert, that is, the worthinesse of the wages and recompence.

4 The merit of congruence, before justification, whereby merit proceedeth or succeedeth our faith, is condemned by the Fathers. Why is it called grace? (saith Augustine in Psal.31.) because it is given gratis. Whosoever is given gratis, it is no more merit, and in his Retractations lib.1. cap.3. he knew not this opinion of merits as a kinde of merit of congruence before justification. I said (quoth he) lib.6. quaest. [ilegible] in religion, salvation never was wrought [ilegible] by any merits: but I said so, as though any man could be worthy by his owne merits, but as the Apostle saith: Not of our workes, but of him that calleth us. And in epist.105. he saith, To make a man just, merit hath not sufficient power. And againe, Righteousnesse in Scripture is never called hire. And in Praefat. in Psal.31. Thou hast not done any good, and yet the forgivenesse of thy sinnes is given thee: And likewise Prosper, sent.6. de object. Gal. saith, The justified man (that is, of unrighteous being made righteous) doth receive a gift without any good merit going before his justification. And Scotus, lib.2. de natur. et grat. cap.4. acknowledgeth that we have in us dispositions unto righteousnesse, but denyeth that they can properly bee called merits. And Stapleton de peccat. orig. lib.2. cap.4. saith, that merit of congruence in respect of the first grace, is long agoe abolished; nor is it allowed of by the most approved schoolemen, as Thomas in his Summe, nor admitted by his followers or latter writers at any time. Indeed Gregory of Arimin. lib.2. dist.26. qu.1. doth expressly condemne it, as Pyralio, in Ioan. and Thomas Waldensis, lib.3. de Sacram.

5 But Merit of condignitie is condemned also by some others: as namely by Augustine, in censure de verb. Apost. Serm.2. in these words: Thou wast not worthy ——— whom hee might glorifie being justified. ——— He crowneth thee in his mercy and pitie, if thou have prevented him by any merits, examine then thy merits (saith God) and thou shalt finde that they are my gifts. Anselme likewise, de mensurat. crux: saith more plainely then any: If a man should serve God with greatest fervencie, a thousand yeares long, yet should not all his deeds be worth the saying one halfe day in heaven. Looke in Gregorie of Arimin, in 1. dist.1. q.1. art.2. Durand, in 2. d.27. q.1. & in 3. d.18. q.2. Waldensis, tom.3. de Sacram. Burgensis, in addit. ad Lyranum super Psal.35. Scotus, in Sent. d.17. q.2. thinketh that our good workes have no proportion with eternall life, and bee therefore accepted of God for reward. You must know (saith Cusanus, serm.19.) that Christs death only was of ability to merit everlasting life, because it being a consummate death, doth merit an excellent life. None of all the other Martyrs doe merit equall with his death, because all other death of whom wee know, comes short of the greatest death, which is in his kinde great, that is, a consummate death, which onely doth merit the greatest (that is, eternall) life.

### Faith

The Fathers affirme that faith justifieth, not as a man [ilegible] by [ilegible] wardly, or preparing him; but by apprehending Christ, and applying of him: which is, when we doe [ilegible] upon the mercy of God and merits of Christ, holding God as favourable unto us within Christ. This is [ilegible] done by God (faith [ilegible] in 1. Cor.) that whosoever beleeveth in Christ shall bee saved without workes, receiving by his only faith free remission of all his sinnes. And Isichius upon Leviticus, lib.4. cap.2. Grace is given out of mercy and compassion, and obtained by faith alone. And Marius Victorinus hath these words upon Gen. 3.

Believ'd, and this sole faith he did confesse, Was held a worthy crowne of righteousnesse: Thus we by Abrahams great reward are taught, By faith in God, true word what good is caught.

As soone as ever a man beleeveth (saith Chrysostome in Rom. 3. hom.7.) he is forthwith justified; and in his commentaries upon the Heb. cap.11. hom.23. after hee hath spoken of the promises made unto the Patriarches, hee addeth, These by their onely faith conceived an assured trust of these things, seeing them a farre off, foure generations: yee they came to passe——. So firmely were they perswaded of them, that they did as it were salute them comming——. Thou seest that this receiving of theirs, was but an expectation and trust of them: if therefore to trust bee to receive, then may we also receive. And it is Augustines opinion in Prosper, In Sent. 352. that the faith of Christ, is to beleeve in him that doth justifie the wicked: to beleeve in the Mediatour without whom no man is reconciled unto God: to beleeve in the Saviour who came to seeke and save that which was lost; to beleeve in him that said, You can do nothing without me. Now what it is to beleeve in him, that justifieth the wicked, the same Father Tract. 29. in Ioan. sayeth downe, saying: What is it then to beleeve in him? In beleeving him to love him, in beleeving him to depend upon him, in beleeving him to turne unto him, and to be incorporated into his bodie: And in other places, and that very often hee useth to affirme that to beleeve in God, is to cleave unto God, and to bend towards God. Looke in his enarration upon the 77. Psalm, in his 54. tractate upon Iohn, and in his 181. Sermon de tempore. Hee also in his 26. Tractate upon Iohn saith, Who so beleeveth in him, receiveth him, and is invisibly fedde; because invisibly regenerate: and in his 50. tractate upon Iohn: How shall I reach my hand unto heaven, and lay hold of him as he sitteth there? why, send but up thy faith, and thou hast hold of him. And Ser.33. de verb. Dom. Behold, we beleeve in Christ whom wee have received through faith: and in our receiving him we know what to thinke upon: we receive but a little, and yet our hearts are fedde fat therewith.

So Bertram in his booke of the bodie and blood of Christ, saith thus; This bodie is not to bee received, beheld, or eaten with the senses of the flesh, but with attention of a faithfull soule——. And the decretals themselves de consecrat. d.2. counsell us in this manner, Behold the holy body and blood of thy Lord with faith, honour and admire it, touch it with thy minde, receive it with the hand of thine heart, and take it as holy with the endeavour of thine inward man. And Lombard Sent. lib.3. dist.19. faith [ilegible] justified by the blood of Christ, namely, that wee are cleansed from our sinnes by the faith of his death: and therefore saith the Apostle, the righteousnesse of God (in us) is through the faith of Iesus Christ, and by and by after he saith, whom God hath made a propitiatour by faith in his blood, that is, by the faith of his passion. If therefore we behold him that died upon the crosse for us, with the eyes of faith, we are loosed from the bands of the devill, that is, from our sinnes.

2 That the justification of our soules, by faith consisteth not in apprehension but in inward preparation and disposition, it is a fantasticke invention of the Schoolemen.

3 The Fathers doe hold faith onely to be requisite unto justification, even without the workes of grace. We must especially beleeve (saith Augustine Serm.181. de temp.) the remission of sinnes; for this is the onely remedie which looseth man from the sentence of death eternall.

4 I am able to shew (saith Chrysostome hom. de fide & lege natur.) that a faithfull man hath both lived in this life without workes, & hath attained unto the kingdome of heaven——. And the theefe beleved onely, and was justified; but I dare affirme that onely faith by it selfe hath saved some. And hom.7. in cap.3. Roman. What is the law of faith? (saith he) to bee saved by grace. Here hee sheweth the power of God, in that he not onely saved us, but also justified and glorified us, and that without use of any workes, exsisting onely faith of us.

Wee have not beleeved of our owne accord, (saith Theodoret in Eph.2.) but came being called, and when we are come, hee doth not exact puritie and innocencie of life, but hath pardoned our sinnes accepting of faith onely.

This it is to glorie in the Lord (saith Basil Serm. de hum.) when a man is not puffed up with his owne righteousnesse, but acknowledgeth himselfe destitute of all true righteousnesse, and justified by faith alone in Iesus Christ.

They are justified before God (saith Ambrose in Roman. 4.) without any labour or toyle, by onely faith, no workes of penitence being hereto required, but onely that they beleeve.

Origen upon the 3. of the Romans, after he hath alledged the example of Paul, saith: Therefore the just cause of mans glorying is in the faith of the crosse of Christ, which excludeth all glorying that proceedeth from the workes of the law.

Augustine against Pelagius his 2. Epistle lib.1. cap.11. faith, that of how great holinesse soever the Saints of either the new or old testament are said to bee, yet nothing saved them but faith in the mediatour, who shed his blood for the remission of their sinnes.

That a man should bee saved by his faith, that hath no good workes, it may bee is not a thing out of custome, saith Chrysostome in Rom 4. hom.8. but to see a man who is noted for good workes, not to be saved by them, but by faith, this is an admirable thing, and doth make a most manifest demonstration of the efficacie and power of faith. And Hom.14. in cap.8. Wee offer but one gift unto God, namely in beleeving his promises of things to come, & by this only way wee are brought unto salvation.

4 Whensoever the Fathers doe joyne faith and workes together, in the matter of our salvation, they speake of an historicall and generall faith, which is onely a knowledge and universall assent, or otherwise of the externall profession of faith, or also of faith as it is the [867] pathway to salvation: for although faith as it is the instrument or meanes to apprehend Christ unto righteousnesse, and salvation, be alone, and unjoyned with any other meane: yet as it is the way unto salvation, it is not alone. Whence we acknowledge that faith alone is not sufficient unto salvation, and to live a good life by, but must have the assistance of good workes and other vertues.

The helpe of repentance, saith Lactantius de divin. instit. epit. cap.9. is great: which whosoever doth cast away, doth barre himselfe of the way to salvation.

Some do purge away their sinnes——— by watching, saith Chrysostome in Ioan. hom.38. thou maist doe this an easier way, namely, by exercising patience unto all men.

By workes of righteousnesse, saith Eucherius in Reg. lib.3. we come to the kingdome of heaven: and, we cannot come to these everlasting joyes, but by faith, and works of justice. And againe, let them begin at faith and continue to the end of their journy in good manners, untill they come whither they intend. in Gen. lib.3.

Let us make pitie our patron in this world, saith Caesarius Hom.15. that it may deliver us in the world to come, for there is mercy in heaven, which is obtained by exercising mercy here upon earth.

Some hasten unto God by fasting, saith Haimo sup. Psal.134.: others by almes; and others by other vertues. Let us hasten unto our countrey in heaven by doing good workes, saith another, viz. Ideot. contemp. lib.2. capite 15. And Rabanus saith there are many fruits of repentance by which a man may attaine unto the clearing of his crimes.

5 Sometimes the Fathers joyning workes to faith, doe speake of faith as it is a perswasion of the impunitie and freedome of sinnes, without penitence or as it is an unperfect vertue, unto which other vertues are therefore to be joyned.

6 The Fathers doe acknowledge a speciall and unfailable certainty of faith in God. Trust in God, saith Remigius Alisiodorensis in Psal.10. that is, All my faith is in Christ? By him onely I beleeve to be justified and saved; he is my rocke, he is my refuge.

He that beleeveth with a strong affection, saith Theophylact doth extend his heart wholly unto God; and what then? hee is united to him. And his heart being enkindled, conceiveth a most certaine assurance to be made partaker of his desire: this doe all men finde true by experience.

If thou beleeve that thy sinnes cannot bee forgiven, saith Bernard in Mar.11. De Antich. Ser.1. but by him whom onely thou didst sinne against, and who himselfe cannot sinne, thou dost well: but adde this, that thou beleevest that by him they may be forgiven, this is the testimonie that the holy Ghost doth set downe in thy heart, saying, Thy sinnes are forgiven thee. And againe epist.107. Who is righteous but hee that recompenseth Gods love with his love againe? And this is never done, but when the holy Ghost by faith revealeth unto man, Gods purpose from everlasting, concerning his future salvation. And Ser.5. Dedica. Here it is most plainly necessarie that faith doe succour us——that that which lieth hidden concerning us in the heart of the Father, may by his Spirit bee revealed unto us, and the same Spirit testifying unto us, may perswade our spirits, that we are the sonnes of God: and may perswade us by calling us, and justifying us freely by faith. And againe elsewhere. We know that we are translated from death to life by this quickening Spirit, and by a certaine and daily experiment (the same spirit enlightning us) we doe prove, that our prayers and contrition doe come from him, and ascend unto God, before whose eyes they doe finde mercy. And in his eight Sermon upon the Canticles. What soule amongst you all (saith hee) hath at sometimes felt the Spirit of the Sonne in his secret conscience, crying, Abba, Father: Let that, O let that soule presume boldly, that it is beloved with a Fatherly affection, that findeth it selfe affected with the same Spirit that affected the Son: trust to it (thou soule whatsoever thou art): trust unto it, & never doubt at any thing. And in his 69. Sermon hee hath these words. Nothing can forbid this soule to say, God is my beloved, which in that it feeles it selfe to love, and to love vehemently, doubts not but that it is beloved, as ardently, and as vehemently: and of the singular intent, desire, care, labour, diligence, and studie, that it shewes forth in endeavouring so incessantly and earnestly to please God, doth undoubtedly acknowledge all these in it selfe, remembring that promise——— therefore by it owne proper affects, it knoweth how God is affected, and doubteth not that it is beloved againe, feeling it selfe doth love.

There is a certaine kind of glorying in a mans conscience (saith Augustine, in Psal.149.) & that is, when thou knowest thy faith to be sincere, thy hope to bee infallible, thy charitie to be unfained. And in his 75. Tractate upon Iob, he saith this saying: For now is he in us, and we in him; but this as how we doe but beleeve, but then we shall know also, although we know it already by beleeving: but then we shall know it by contemplating. And in another place, in his 13. booke of the Trinitie, chap.1. and 2. hee saith, Every man that beleeveth, seeth faith to be in his heart, and he that beleeveth not, seeth that faith is not in his heart.

The minde that is replenished with the holy Ghost (saith Gregorie, Dial. lib.1. chap.1.) hath most evident signes thereof, namely, vertues and humilitie: which if they doe perfectly concurre in one minde, it is certaine that they doe bring assured testimonie of the presence of the holy Ghost. And in the sixt booke of his Register, chap.187. The soule that thirsteth for God, is first touched with feare, and, then with love. But when the feare is worne out with the continuall languishment of sorrow, it at last entreth some securitie and hope of the presuming of pardon. And in his Morals, lib.31. cap.23. he saith, that the securitie of the righteous man, is fitly compared unto a lyon: who when he seeth any come against him, betakes himselfe to his wonted courage: so the other knoweth that hee shall overcome all adversaries, because he loveth him onely, whom against his will he can never fall from.

There is abiding in us (saith Cyprian, ad Demet.) a fortitude of hope, and a firmenesse of faith, and an upright and vigorous heart, (even amongst the greatest ruines of this declining world) and a patience alwaies rejoycing, and a soule alwaies secure of the favour of his God. And de Cena elsewhere: Our affection knowing it selfe cured and sanctified, washeth it selfe with teares.——And in his (Gods) presence these well-wished teares doe begge for pardon.

Let the hearts of the faithfull (saith Zeno Sermon 10. de quadr.) examine themselves, ——— that finding in themselves any fruits of charitie laid up, they may know without all doubt that God is in them. And Serm.8. de Epiphan. He that will trie whither God doe dwell within him or no, ——— if he doe diligently examine the inward parts of his heart, and doe finde therein the love of God and his neighbour, assuredly, and without dissimulation, hee needeth nor doubt that God both governeth him and dwelleth in him.

Hee gave him for vs (saith Ambrose, de Iacob. & vit. beat. lib.1. cap.6.) therefore there is no doubt that we need feare any thing should be denied us, there is no cause for us to doubt of the continuance of Gods munificence towards us. And againe, Serm.2. in Psal.118. He that hath a good conscience, is not troubled nor in doubt, but constantly affirmeth, Wee be the heires of God, and joynt-heires with Christ. And in one of the sermons under his name, he saith, whosoever doth sticke fast unto that leaven Christ, shall also be convoyed into heaven, as well helpefull to himselfe, as convenient unto others, and certaine of his salvation, and secure of the calling and gaining of others.

By this, that the holy Ghost doth infuse charitie into us (saith Anselme, in Rom.8.) hee declareth unto our hearts by an evident testimony that we are the children of God. And in 1 Cor.2. Wee know by his spirit, that wee have both his gifts, and also received them of him. And againe, He that hath the feeling of faith in his heart, this man knoweth that Christ is in him. in 1 Cor.13.

Whensoever any man feeleth himselfe so affected either with his owne sins, or with others as we have said, saith Basil Reg. constrail. q.196. then [griego] let him undoubtedly know, that he is free from sinne.

And Cyrill upon Iohn lib.10. cap.3. besides this generall knowledge doth also set downe another, namely, by which the faithfull having received illumination from the spirit, do with the eyes of their minde see God dwelling in them. This is not (saith he) the common and generall knowledge of the Saints, but another, farre more cleare, and more certaine, and farre differing from that other generall knowledge.

Let us bring faith and obedience (saith Chrysostome, in Gen. cap.29. hom.54.) and beleeve as confidently upon Gods promises, as though they were already performed: and againe in Rom.8. hom.14. Seeing we have the testimonie of that supreme essence, who giveth us what hee promiseth, and also commandeth us to aske, who can from henceforth doubt of this dignitie?

When these three are sealed in the minde (saith Hales, sup.2. dist.12. q.20.) light, gladnesse, and peace, it is a most sure experiment that the soule hath grace.

Yea Thomas Aquinas 1 2. q.112. art.5. and the most ancient of the schoolemen, doe either deny the certainty of knowledge then of faith. I beleeve that I have faith (saith Scotus lib.3. dist.23.) and so affirme all the moderne writers. The Enchiridion of Colen teacheth that it is necessary unto justification for every one to beleeve certainly that his sinnes are forgiven him. So Catharinus teacheth and defendeth that the faithfull may have assurance of faith concerning grace in this life. And Cajet. in Rom.8. saith, that the testimonie of the spirit is a gift by which I neither see, nor know; but I beleeve that I am the sonne of God. So Martinus the Carmelite Frier in his oration unto the Councell of Trent, Anno 1546. saith; Let a man abhorre the fruitlesse confidence in his owne worth, and depend wholly upon Gods mercy; let him hold God to be alwaies present with him as a most mercifull Father, from whom he is alwaies to expect all joy, and all felicity, nor ought he ever to let this perswasion goe out of his minde, although he be molested with the most intolerable and infinite difficulties that the world, the flesh, and the divell can any waies inflict, to withdraw us from our trust upon God and his divine worship. And, Wherefore they never wander in the Labyrinth of doubt, that have obtained righteousnesse through Christ: but living in securitie of conscience, in peace of minde, in joy of heart, and taught by that Spirit which testifieth unto them that they are the sonnes of God, they dare be bold to say, Abba Father.

7 Where the Fathers doe sometimes seeme to deny the speciall assurance of faith, they doe speake of presumption, or the carnall security wherein men doe dreame of liberty and peace without temptation and hazard. Which of all the company of the faithfull (saith S. Augustin. de cor. et grat. cap. 13.) dares presume that hee is of the numbers of the predestinate, as long as he liveth here, upon earth?

Sometimes they speake of the certainty of continuance unto the end without fall or defect: and in this sense saith Augustine De civit. Dei lib. 11. cap. 12. Who is hee that knoweth that he shall persever in increase and acts of justice untill the end? unlesse he be instructed of this by revelation from him that instructeth all concerning this matter by his just and secret judgement, and deceiveth no man.

Sometimes they speake of the assurance of experience, which is alwayes after the event of the thing. Sometimes of the certainty of grace and salvation of others. Sometimes of assurance by speciall revelation, or priviledged assurance, not the ordinary certainty contained in the word & sacraments. Sometimes of the demonstrative assurance, begetting knowledge in the minde, by peculiar and proper principles, not of the assurance of faith. And sometimes of that certainty which is without any signes or tokens, called the certainty of Evidence.

8 The speciall and particular assurance of faith was never condemned for heresie, before the Councill of Trent condemned it.

__________
[867] Augus. Retract. l.1. c.14. vid fidei.

### Fulfilling of the Law. Supererogation.

1 The Fathers doe affirme the law to bee fulfilled, first by imputing the obedience of Christ by faith; and then, by beginning to worke it, and endeavouring either according to ability, not perfectly: or in the perfection of parts, but not of degrees.

Testimonies.

All the commandements of God are accomplished also bee fulfilled, when whatsoever is not done is pardoned. Augustine, Retract. lib. 1. cap. 19.

Then are we just (saith Hier. lib. 1. c. 2. contr. Pelag.) when wee confesse our selves sinners, and our justice consisteth not in, our proper merits, but in the mercies of God, looke the first booke of Bernard, de Vita. cap. 13.

He that beleeveth in Christ (saith Theodoret, in Rom. 10.) doth fulfill the scope of the law. What will the law doe, (saith Chrysostome, in Rom. 10. Hom. 17.) make a man justifie cannot: for none did ever fulfill it.

Hee hath obtained the perfection of the law, saith Sedulius in Rom. 10. who beleeveth in Christ, for seeing none is justified by the law, because none hath fulfilled the law, faith was set downe to satisfie for all omissions in the whole law.

No man ever fulfilled the law (saith Cassianus, Eremit. lib. 10.) which consisteth in love, but hee alone that came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfill it.

2 Now, that there are two wayes of fulfilling the law properly and perfectly without any breach, one in this present life, and another in the life to come, none that I ever heard of, but the schoolemen did never teach. For the ancient Doctors doe acknowledge no perfection at all in this life, but onely that which consisteth in acknowledging our imperfection and enormities. So saith S. Augustine, cont. 2. ep. Pelag. l. 3. c. 7. That vertue which is in a man which is just, in this life is called perfect with this proviso, that unto the perfection thereof, there doe also belong both a true knowledge, and an humble confession of the imperfection thereof. And in ep. 29. ad Hieron. Such Charity—as cannot bee increased in this life, is in no man: and as long as it may be increased, that which is lesse then it ought to be, is of corruption, by reason of which there is not one just man upon earth that doth good, & sinneth not. By which corruption it commeth to passe, that no living man shall bee justified in Gods sight. And de perfecta justi. resp. ad Rusticum. 17. he saith: As long as there is any reliques of carnall concupiscence remaining—God is not wholly beloved, nor with the whole heart; for the flesh without the soule hath no concupiscence. But in his booke, de Spiritu & litera, the last chapter, hee seemeth to hold a contrary opinion; for there he saith, that here there cannot bee so much love of God as is due unto a full & perfect knowledge, this is not for all that to bee accounted as a sinne. But for the reconciliation of these two places, wee must know that there is two sorts of faults: the one when a thing is done directly opposite unto Gods will, and by him forbidding the other when that is done which God commandeth, but not altogether with the whole heart, as he commaundeth: and this Augustine speaketh not, but of the other in the latter quotation, & contrariwise of the former in the first.

3 We are not satisfied by workes (saith [ilegible]) but by faith, because our owne infirmity doth hinder our workes.

The Saints themselves (quoth Bernard, in Cant. Serm. 73.) had need to pray for their sinnes, that they may have salvation through mercy, and not in trusting to their owne righteousnesse. And againe, [ilegible]: How should that bee commaunded, which could not possibly be fulfilled? Why? If you will have it to concerne onely the office of Christ, I will not stand in contention with you, so that you graunt thus much to me, that it cannot, nor ever shall be fulfilled in this life, by any man.

We can hardly doe one good worke (saith Radulphus, in Levit. lib. 1. c. 1.) without intermission of some sinne or other with it, and it is to be feared, lest when wee looke for a complete reward of devotion, the punishment for the fault therewith conjoyned, bee not exacted of us.

3 Supererogation, wherein a good worke of counsell done over and beyond the fulfilling of the law, is acceptable unto God, was a stranger unto the knowledge of the Fathers: For although they say that virginitie is offered more then due, and above the lawes; and that many doe exceede the commandements with their worke, and performe more in duty then the precepts doe bind them to; yet that the law is so kept, that the keepers are not transgressours; they doe not say; I affirme againe, they do not say so. But they will have supererogative workes done, not that there can bee any duty done which is beyond the morall law, but these workes they holde may surpasse, first the negative part: for so saith Chrysostome, Hom. 8. in Rom. 4. Not to steale or kill, is in every mans power: but to beleeve that God can doe that which is otherwise impossible, this requires a minde elevated, and a more vehement affection towards God. For this is a signe of a worthy and noble love. He honours God that keepes his Commaundements; but he much more that can argue and dispute through his faith: the other obeyeth God, but this doth ascribe him—his glory with greater measure and vehemency.

Secondly, they held supererogation above externall acts, and in this sense Chrysost. Hom. 3. in 1 Cor. doth speake, when he determineth that the Philosophers had supererogation: Are not his precepts so easie (quoth he) that many have gone beyond them by philosophicall reason?

Thirdly, they held it as it exceedeth some one commandement. So is Augustines saying, understood of the virgins, Serm. 8. de verb. Apost. The virgins (quoth he) did labour for the beauty of the heart: What doest thou command us? to abstaine from adultery, dost thou command us this? wee doe performe more in loving thee then thou commaundest us, in this commandement.

Lastly, as it exceedeth the commandement which is common unto other men. The Apostle Paul did spend more (saith Augustine, de opere Monachor. cap. 5.) because (as himselfe witnesseth) he warred at his owne charges.

Virginity is a voluntary thing (saith [ilegible], Parm.) and not of the necessity. S. Paul gave not any precept, but onely counselleth us unto virginity. So doe some of the other Fathers account virginity above the law; that is, above the ordinary observation of the law among other Christians, because they thought it to be an Angelicall state. But yet Ambrose, libro de Virginitate, doth plainly put virginity from amongst the counsels, and in the Precepts. What man, saith he, either in his life, or after his death, hath beene the author of keeping virginity?——yet our Saviour Christ the King of all men, prevailed thus much in this kinde of commandements, that children not being of maturity to receive the discipline of the Lawes, should professe virginity which is above the lawes. And in his Apology to Constantius, That holy and heavenly command of eternall virginity is not kept nor fulfilled happily, but onely among us Christians.

4 This kinde of supererogation, which the Papists now teach, is in some sort reproved by some of the Fathers.

None can restore so much as hee oweth, saith Anselme, de concep. Virg. c. 21. onely Christ restored for all that are saved, more then hee ought. And Thom. in 2.2. quaest. 184. art. 3. will have perfection to consist really and essentially in the keeping of the commandements, and instrumentally in the exercising of the counsels: and for this purpose alleageth the words of Abbot Moyses: Fastings, watchings, &c. are not perfection it selfe, but the instruments of perfection, because that the ende of that discipline doth not consist in them, but they are the meanes to bring us unto that end.

### Pilgrimage.

1 Religious Pilgrimage got footing after Constantines time, about the yeare of grace 320. and yet was not as then used by al, but only by the vulgar; not undertaken for any worship of God, or merit sake, but onely for confirmation of faith. It is a part of faith (saith Hierome epist. 154.) to worship the ground whereupon Christs feet did tread. Severus Sulpitius, histor. libro secundo, and Paulinus, Paulinum, epist. ad Sever. saith, that mens minds doe draw them to Hierusalem for no other cause, but only to see, and to touch the places wherein Christ was corporally present.

And before Constantines time, it is told as a rare thing of Alexander, and a wonderfull, that he hasted unto Hierusalem, to worship and visite the holy places, as Eusebius recordeth, lib. 6. cap. 19. But marke there that all this was doone by a vision.

2. Afterward, succeeding times changed these pilgrimages into part of Gods worship and religion; but yet the most orthodoxall Fathers in that respect did alwaies condemne it. So doth Nyssenus in an epistle of his affirming that it addeth not a iotte unto piety, and that God is present to those that call upon his name, in every place alike. The Lord saith not, saith Aug. Serm. de Mart. 3. inter Serm. de Sanct. goe into the East, and seeke justice, or sayle into the West to receive pardon: forgive thine enemy, and thou shalt be forgiven: Doe not seeke ought of thy selfe, without thy selfe. God doth direct thee unto thy selfe, and thine owne conscience.

Hildebertus Cenomanensis in an epistle to a certaine Count, doth affirme, that Pilgrimage is an inexcusable sin in them that are bound unto any ministery; and likewise to preferre things not necessary, before things necessary: and things not due, before duties: and to wander about the world, no Doctour, no Scripture doth at any time, or in any place mention.
